a6a1b23ed98fc7d7: KUALA LUMPUR: Natasha Roslan may have fallen short of retaining her IBF World Cup women's singles crown, but reaching a second consecutive final has given the Malaysian bowler plenty of positives to take into the team competition in Munich, Germany.
The 2025 champion, who made history by capturing gold in Hong Kong, settled for silver after going down 2-1 to France's Manon Clement in Sunday's final.
Clement took the opening game 231-190 before Natasha responded superbly to level the contest with a 206-147 victory.
However, the Frenchwoman prevailed 204-168 in the decider to deny Natasha back-to-back titles.
Despite falling at the final hurdle, Natasha was proud of her achievement, having followed up last year's historic triumph with another impressive run to the title match.
"So close yet so far to defend my title. Of course, I would have loved to win again, but I'm still happy, grateful, and proud to finish second," said Natasha.
"I gave it my best, and there's a lot I can take from this to keep improving."
Natasha's latest silver further underlined her consistency on the international stage, coming three years after she became Malaysia's first women's singles world champion in Kuwait in 2023.
Her road to the final began with convincing 2-0 victories over the Netherlands' Samantha Greiner (172-168, 189-168) and compatriot Sin Li Jane (258-178, 203-195).
She then had to dig deep in the quarter-finals against Denmark's Karen Kaergaard Nielsen, who had earlier eliminated two other Malaysians, Nur Hazirah Ramli and Adelia Nur Irwan Syazalee.
After dropping the opening game 201-191, Natasha recovered to win the next two (216-177, 196-180) and secure a place in the semi-finals.
She followed up with another assured display, defeating Sweden's Nora Johansson 211-157, 201-192 to book her place in the final.

The other Malaysian women also put up commendable performances, with Li Jane opening her knockout campaign with a convincing 2-0 victory over Denmark's Megan Dicay, winning 258-170, 218-168, before losing to Natasha in the last 16.
Adelia battled past the Philippines' Krizziah Lyn Macatula 2-1 in the last 32, but her challenge ended with a 2-0 defeat to Nielsen, who prevailed 212-207, 220-183.
Nur Hazirah also gave Nielsen a tough fight in the last 32 before going down 2-1. The Dane took the opening game 224-200, lost the second 213-171, but bounced back to clinch the decider 250-166.
With the singles competition concluded, Natasha will now shift her focus to the team event alongside Li Jane, Adelia and Nur Hazirah.
The quartet will be hoping to go one better than Malaysia's silver medal-winning women's team at last year's World Cup, when they suffered a narrow 3-2 defeat to the United States in the final.
"Next up is the team event, so the focus now is to reset and get ready with the girls," said Natasha, who remains determined to help Malaysia challenge for another medal.
"Still more to fight for," she added, as Malaysia look to challenge for another medal.

a5193db88469bc20: KUALA LUMPUR: The lively atmosphere at the wedding reception of Bella Astillah and Muar MP Syed Saddiq Syed Abdul Rahman last night turned emotional when Bella's nine-year-old son, Mohamed Ayden Adrean, delivered a touching speech.

Dressed in matching red traditional Malay attire alongside his six-year-old sister, Ara Adreanna, Ayden took to the stage at the Malaysia International Trade and Exhibition Centre (MITEC) to offer prayers for the newly married couple and thank Syed Saddiq for bringing happiness back into their lives.

Speaking calmly despite the emotion in his voice, Ayden shared his heartfelt thoughts: "I am Ayden, and from the bottom of my heart, I want to say to Daddy that you came into our lives when I was very little, and at times I did not quite understand what was happening. I only saw Mommy being sad. As a son, I now see Mommy smiling again, and with your presence, she laughs a lot and is truly happy."
"Thank you for choosing Mommy and giving us our happiness back," he added.

"Mommy, I love you so much for taking such good care of us. To Daddy, thank you for loving us and Mommy. May Allah bless Mommy and Daddy's marriage. Ara and I love you both very much, Mommy and Daddy."
The grand celebration was attended by around 3,000 guests, including government ministers and prominent national leaders.
Later in the evening, the couple changed out of their traditional red outfits into a sleek black suit and an elegant white gown.
Guests were entertained by performances from National Songbird Datuk Seri Siti Nurhaliza, Jaclyn Victor, Didi Astillah, and Nidji frontman Muhammad Yusuf Nur Ubay.
Syed Saddiq, 34, and Bella, 32, officially tied the knot in a solemnisation ceremony at Menara Merdeka Maybank on Oct 10.
The couple will host two further Kenduri Rakyat wedding receptions in their respective hometowns of Muar, Johor, on Oct 25 and Kota Kinabalu, Sabah, on Oct 31.
b1f2325ace5d6b5f: PETALING JAYA: Political analysts say parties are reluctant to contest elections on their own due to the electoral consequences of vote-splitting and concerns about exposing internal weaknesses.
Syaza Shukri of the International Islamic University Malaysia said fragmentation of the Malay vote represented the parties’ “biggest fear”, especially for Umno and PAS.
“If the Malay vote is split, they may still win, but it could be a repeat of the 2021 Melaka state election, where more than a third of the seats were won by slim majorities.

"People might then question the legitimacy (of the winning party). The idea of (Umno and PAS) working together is to show they have the people’s mandate, so they can effectively defeat Pakatan Harapan," she told FMT.

Syaza was commenting on a suggestion by Umno Supreme Council member Puad Zarkashi that all political coalitions and parties contest the Melaka polls on their own to gauge their actual strength ahead of GE16.

Analyst Ahmad Zaharuddin Sani Ahmad Sabri of Global Asia Consulting said political parties that contest independently risk discovering that their actual level of support is considerably smaller than what their leaders claim.
"A party that regularly pushes for a large share of seats may discover that its (actual) electoral influence does not justify its demands," he said.

Zaharuddin also said smaller parties may lack sufficient candidates, funding, election machinery and grassroots networks to compete effectively across constituencies, while other parties may fear that a poor result would weaken their bargaining position ahead of GE16.
Melaka: the right testing ground
Syaza said both BN and Perikatan Nasional (PN) can use the upcoming Melaka election to determine which side commands the support of the Malay electorate in the state.
"We know that if they work together, they can secure a large percentage of the Malay vote, but we would not know whether that support is driven primarily by Umno or PAS,” she said.
However, Syaza said that if both parties contest independently and PAS emerges as the more influential force, it may no longer be accurate to speak of a “blue wave”.

Zaharuddin said that Melaka offers a valuable political testing ground, with the results of the preceding state election offering a useful benchmark for parties to assess their electoral gains and losses.
In 2021, BN won 21 state assembly seats, followed by PH (5) and PN (two).

"However, the real value of going solo extends beyond counting seats. It allows parties to examine their actual appeal, organisational strength, candidate quality and ability to attract voters beyond their traditional support base.
"Coalitions can sometimes create an illusion of strength by combining different voter bases.
“Contesting independently helps reveal which parties possess genuine grassroots support and which depend heavily on the machinery, reputation or electoral appeal of their partners," he said.
PAS, PH should go solo
Syaza expects PAS in particular to contest the Melaka state polls on its own despite its push for ummah unity with Umno and BN. She said doing so could strengthen the party’s bargaining position.
PAS currently holds two of Melaka's six parliamentary seats, Tangga Batu and Jasin, while BN failed to win a single seat in GE15.
She added that PAS could gain leverage in future negotiations with BN if it were to outperform Umno, as it did in GE15.
"But if they lose and BN forms the government in Melaka, it will just be status quo. It’s not like PAS would be losing a state.”
Zaharuddin believes PH should also contest independently in Melaka, particularly if it wants to establish a credible foundation for GE16.

"PH needs to know whether voters continue to support its reform agenda, whether its component parties will retain their respective constituencies, and whether it can persuade undecided voters that it offers a credible alternative government," he said.
b76c3c83f4eab5c4: PETALING JAYA: Kecenderungan parti politik keberatan bertanding solo pada pilihan raya menjurus kebimbangan berlakunya perpecahan undi, kata penganalisis.
Syaza Shukri dari Universiti Islam Antarabangsa Malaysia, berkata perpecahan undi orang Melayu merupakan 'ketakutan terbesar', terutama Umno dan PAS.
“Sekiranya undi orang Melayu berpecah, mereka mungkin masih boleh menang, tetapi ia akan menjadi ulangan PRN Melaka 2021, di mana lebih satu pertiga daripada kerusi dimenangi majoritinya tipis.

"Rakyat mungkin akan mempersoalkan keabsahan (parti menang). Idea untuk (Umno dan PAS) bekerjasama adalah untuk menunjukkan mereka mendapat mandat rakyat, sekali gus membolehkan Pakatan Harapan (PH) ditumpaskan sepenuhnya," katanya kepada FMT.
Syaza mengulas cadangan bekas ahli Majlis Kerja Tertinggi Umno, Puad Zarkashi, supaya semua gabungan dan parti politik bertanding solo pada PRN Melaka bagi menguji kekuatan sebenar menjelang PRU16.

Ahmad Zaharuddin Sani Ahmad Sabri dari Global Asia Consulting, berkata parti politik bertanding solo berdepan risiko mendapati tahap sokongan sebenar jauh lebih kecil, berbanding dakwaan pemimpin sendiri.
"Parti yang sering mendesak mendapatkan pembahagian kerusi yang besar mungkin mendapati pengaruh (sebenar) pada pilihan raya tidak sepadan dengan tuntutan," katanya.

Zaharuddin berkata, parti kecil mungkin kekurangan calon, dana, jentera pilihan raya, dan rangkaian akar umbi yang mencukupi bertanding secara bermakna di semua kawasan Parlimen atau DUN, manakala parti lain mungkin bimbang keputusan buruk akan melemahkan kedudukan rundingan menjelang PRU16.
Melaka jadi medan uji kaji
Syaza berkata, BN dan Perikatan Nasional (PN) dapat menggunakan PRN Melaka akan datang menentukan pihak mana yang menguasai sokongan pengundi Melayu di negeri itu.
"Kita tahu jika mereka bekerjasama, mereka boleh meraih peratusan undi Melayu yang besar, namun kita tidak tahu sama ada sokongan itu didorong Umno atau PAS,” katanya.
Bagaimanapun, Syaza berkata, jika dua parti itu bertanding solo dengan PAS muncul kuasa lebih berpengaruh, pandangan mengenai 'gelombang biru' mungkin tidak lagi tepat.
Zaharuddin pula berkata, Melaka menawarkan medan ujian politik yang bernilai, di mana keputusan PRN menjadi penanda aras berguna bagi parti politik menilai untung dan rugi.
Pada 2021, BN menang 21 DUN, diikuti PH (5), dan PN (dua).

"Namun, nilai sebenar bertanding solo jauh lebih daripada sekadar mengira jumlah kerusi. Ia membolehkan parti mengukur daya tarikan sebenar, kekuatan organisasi, kualiti calon serta keupayaan mereka menarik pengundi di luar asas sokongan tradisi.
"Gabungan politik kadang-kala boleh mewujudkan ilusi kekuatan dengan menggabungkan asas pengundi berbeza.

“Bertanding solo membantu mendedahkan parti mana yang mempunyai sokongan tulen akar umbi dan parti mana yang sangat bergantung kepada jentera, reputasi atau daya tarikan pilihan raya rakan kongsi mereka," katanya.
PAS, PH patut tanding solo

Syaza menjangkakan PAS akan bertanding PRN Melaka secara solo walaupun parti itu terus mendesak agar perpaduan ummah dicapai bersama Umno dan BN. Beliau berkata, langkah itu dapat mengukuhkan kedudukan rundingan parti tersebut.
PAS kini memegang dua daripada enam kerusi Parlimen di Melaka, iaitu Tangga Batu dan Jasin, manakala BN gagal menang sebarang kerusi pada PRU15.
Beliau berkata, PAS berpeluang memperoleh kelebihan dalam rundingan masa hadapan dengan BN, jika dapat mengatasi prestasi Umno sebagaimana yang berlaku pada PRU15.
"Tetapi, jika mereka kalah dan BN membentuk kerajaan Melaka, ia hanya kekal sebagai status quo. Lagipun, PAS bukannya hilang satu negeri."
Dalam pada itu, Zaharuddin percaya PH juga sepatutnya bertanding solo di Melaka, andai mahu membina asas kukuh menjelang PRU16.

"PH perlu mengetahui sama ada pengundi masih menyokong agenda reformasi, sama ada parti komponennya mampu mengekalkan kawasan DUN masing-masing, dan sama ada ia dapat meyakinkan pengundi yang belum membuat keputusan bahawa ia menawarkan kerajaan alternatif berwibawa," katanya.
dcfb8fb230df2928: KUALA LUMPUR: When a pet owner posted on social media that their cat had died during the haze, the claim moved other animal lovers to raise an uncomfortable question - how much can polluted air affect our pets?

While a single case cannot establish that haze was responsible for an animal’s death, veterinarian Dr Muhammad Naim Kasim said cats and dogs can suffer respiratory effects when fine particles enter their airways.
“Pets have the same respiratory system as humans. When the environment is unhealthy due to haze, with dust and impurities in the air, it can affect the lung health of cats and dogs," he said.

Fine particles can irritate the respiratory tract and trigger inflammation, potentially making it harder for an animal to breathe. Naim said pet owners should pay attention to changes such as breathing difficulties and watery eyes, although these symptoms can have other causes and need veterinary assessment.

Animals with existing respiratory problems such as asthma may be particularly vulnerable during periods of poor air quality. Older pets and those with heart disease may also have less ability to cope when breathing becomes more difficult.

“My advice is that if we know our pets have heart disease, respiratory problems or other health conditions, try not to take them outdoors,” Naim added. “Keep them indoors and ensure that the air quality at home is good.”

Staying inside does not necessarily eliminate exposure, however: haze particles can enter homes through open windows and doors, so indoor air quality can still deteriorate when conditions outside are poor.
For pets accustomed to roaming outdoors, keeping them inside temporarily may be worthwhile when haze becomes severe, particularly if they already have a health condition.
Naim cautioned that prolonged exposure to polluted air could worsen inflammation in the lungs if an affected animal does not receive appropriate treatment.
"Similar to humans, if we spend a long time outdoors in a hazy environment and continuously breathe polluted air without prompt treatment, the inflammation can worsen," he explained.
"If left untreated for too long, there is a possibility that the animal could die."

The important point for owners is not to assume that every cough, watery eye or breathing problem is caused by haze. Those signs can occur with a range of illnesses, and an examination may be needed to determine what is actually wrong.

Animals struggling to breathe may require oxygen therapy, while medication depends on the underlying problem. Anti-inflammatory drugs may be used in some cases, while antibiotics would be appropriate if a bacterial infection is involved.
Ultimately, if your cat or dog appears to be struggling for breath, veterinary attention should not be delayed.
9770a1c665c680c5: TIRANA: Albanian police fired water cannon and tear gas Sunday as violent anti-government protests entered a sixth day and prime minister Edi Rama rejected demonstrators' demands that he resign.
Violent demonstrations have rocked Tirana since Tuesday with protesters calling for action over poor university conditions, high tuition fees and corruption.
Hundreds of protesters gathered again at noon in front of the education ministry chanting "Rama, resign" amid a tense standoff with police.
After police bid to disperse the crowds the protests scattered across the city centre, escalating in hours-long violent clashes.

Protesters set ablaze litter bins in the streets, smashed windows, including at the headquarters of the governing Socialist party, and set fire to a police station and the entrance of the interior ministry.

Chaotic clashes extended to the main boulevard and square with demonstrators throwing rocks, Molotov cocktails and firing pyrotechnic devices, as the police responded with rubber bullets and tear gas, according to an AFP journalist.
Ambulances were seen rushing in and out of the scenes of clashes to pick up the injured.
The ministry of Health told AFP that 16 police officers were injured - 14 of them when protesters attacked the police station.

Albert Nushi, from the police public security department said on Sunday evening that a police station in Tirana was attacked with Molotov cocktails and pyrotechnic devices that endangered both officers and people held in custody.
"An attack on a police station is not a protest. Violence against police officers, attacks on institutions, and actions that endanger human lives cannot be tolerated," he said.
He urged protesters to stay away from masked individuals behind the violence and "assemble in a peaceful manner".
According to the ministry of health, 28 people were injured on Sunday - 19 police officers, four protesters, four passers-by and a journalist.
Before the protest, shops and offices in the city centre secured their doors and windows with metal shutters, while city workers removed paving stones to prevent them being thrown by protesters.
In a video broadcast lasting more than an hour, Rama ruled out resigning, stating that the protests are the "work of an outside hand".
According to Austrian federal press service Rama’s official visit to Federal Chancellor Christian Stocker scheduled for Monday, has been cancelled by the Albanian side.
Buildings on fire
Writer and activist Lura Elezi, 38, told AFP that she is protesting for "a better life, rule of law and against crime and corruption".

"I love my country, but my government does not respect us - it defies us. Every citizen must take responsibility for their country, taking on the duty to lead, to love, and not to destroy one's own nation", she said.

Tirana saw its harshest violence on Saturday when protesters threw rocks, Molotov cocktails, metal objects and pyrotechnic devices at police, and torched cars and litter bins to use as barricades against advancing police.
Buildings including a court, banks and a post office were set on fire or severely damaged.
According to a health ministry report issued Sunday, 65 people were injured, including 37 police, with 12 people hospitalized during Saturday’s protests.
Since Tuesday, 272 people have been injured in the clashes, including 169 police, the ministry said.
Albania's close ally the United States reacted late Saturday. Its embassy in Tirana urged "restraint and calm on all sides".
The European Commission in a written statement “condemned the use of violence in Tirana and other cities”, adding that the response to it “must remain proportionate”.
"In a candidate country firmly committed to the EU accession process... grievances should be handled through constructive dialogue and in a peaceful manner," the statement said.
The unrest follows months of anti-government protests in the Balkan nation, initially sparked by a controversial resort development linked to US president Donald Trump's family.
739c8a26d6904205: KUALA LUMPUR: MBSB Bhd is exploring further acquisitions, including mortgage portfolios, credit card businesses and takaful operations, as it seeks to expand its domestic presence and achieve greater economies of scale.
Chairman Datuk Wan Kamaruzaman Wan Ahmad said the group is considering acquiring financial institutions or selected assets from other industry players as part of its longer-term growth strategy.
"We are looking at all those possibilities and angles," he told Business Times in an interview.
Wan Kamaruzaman said MBSB is particularly interested in exploring mortgage portfolios, while a credit card business could be established organically or acquired from an existing operator.

Its wholly owned banking subsidiary, MBSB Bank Bhd, currently offers debit cards but is not listed as a credit card issuer by Bank Negara Malaysia, making the segment a potential new avenue for growth.
Takaful operations are another potential area of expansion, said Wan Kamaruzaman.

He said any potential acquisition would have to complement MBSB's existing operations and strategic requirements, with the group's Islamic banking focus limiting its options to Syariah-compliant businesses.
Nevertheless, he said opportunities existed among smaller, specialised financial services providers, including operators whose shareholders might be looking to exit their investments.
Asked whether MBSB would consider acquisitions overseas, Wan Kamaruzaman said the group would remain focused on Malaysia for now, with no immediate plans to expand abroad.
He said the group would consider international expansion only when it had achieved sufficient size and financial strength.
The potential acquisitions form part of MBSB's efforts to build greater scale in an increasingly competitive banking industry.
"Banking is about scale. And when you don't have scale, you need to know your niche," he said.
Wan Kamaruzaman said MBSB has the potential to grow its asset base to between RM100 billion and RM120 billion over the longer term.
He said a larger balance sheet would allow the group to benefit from economies of scale, improve operating efficiency and generate better returns.
MBSB's total assets stood at RM69.1 billion as of end June.
Still, Wan Kamaruzaman said the group would remain cautious in expanding its financing portfolio to avoid accumulating further impaired financing.
The group's gross impaired financing improved slightly to 6.23 per cent as of end June, from 6.33 per cent as of end of 2025. However, this was higher than the 5.33 per cent as of end 2024.
It is also higher than the banking industry level of around two per cent.
MBSB has the backing of its major shareholders, the Employees Provident Fund and Permodalan Nasional Bhd, an important advantage in pursuing its longer-term ambitions.
The potential expansion comes as MBSB prepares a new four-year strategic plan covering 2027 to 2030, as its existing FLIGHT26 transformation programme comes to an end.

MBSB previously expanded through the acquisition of Asian Finance Bank in 2018, which established its Islamic banking platform, followed by the acquisition of Malaysian Industrial Development Finance Bhd in 2023.
The group is still working to improve integration and operating efficiency following those acquisitions.
Wan Kamaruzaman said MBSB's next phase of growth would require a combination of scale, prudent financing decisions and a clear focus on businesses where it could compete effectively.

dcddf67c9a6364c8: KUALA LUMPUR: Gamuda Bhd has been in the news for securing billions of ringgit of contracts. In fact, in the financial year ended July 31, 2026 (FY26) alone, the construction group has secured RM36 billion worth of new contracts.
That number has fueled market optimism for Gamuda's share price since March 31. Between then and October 16, Gamuda's share price increased by 28.7 per cent to close at RM4.78 per share.

However, some observers pointed out that the market is too optimistic on Gamuda's earnings prospects. While the group had secured triple the value of construction jobs in FY26 compared with in FY24, its margins have been declining.

It is also worth noting that about a year ago, the market had expected for Gamuda to record about RM1.8 billion of net profits in FY26. On Aug 19, 2025, the counter hit RM5.80 apiece, the highest since the stock was split on Dec 19, 2024.
The counter then went on a prolonged decline to RM3.70 on March 31, some 36.2 per cent lower, as it became clear that Gamuda could not meet the earnings forecast.

This raises the question whether Gamuda can meet the earnings forecast for the financial year ending July 31, 2027 (FY27) of RM1.4 billion, based on the consensus estimates of analysts covering the stock.

"Yes, Gamuda's margins have been declining, and moving forward if there were to be any margin lift, it's not going to be big. Say FY26 margin was five per cent, maybe FY27 only slightly higher at 5.2 per cent," says an analyst with a bank's research outlet.

Gamuda's net profit margins in FY26 was 5.98 per cent, which was the lowest over the last six financial years. In FY21, Gamuda's net profit margins was 17.97 per cent, when the group earned RM632.19 million out of RM3.52 billion revenue.
Except for in FY22 when Gamuda's net margins jumped to 24.21 per cent due to a one-off exceptional gain from the disposal of its highway assets, the rate has been declining year over year.

The declining margin coincides with Gamuda's expansions overseas. In FY21, overseas revenue was RM705.3 million, or 16.4 per cent of total, while net profit was RM97.6 million, making up 19.9 per cent of the total.

In FY26, total overseas revenue stood at RM11.07 billion, or 59.5 per cent of total. However, overseas net profits were only RM514.06 million, or 48.9 per cent of the total, despite contributing the larger portion to total revenue.

This shows that net profit margin of Gamuda's overseas ventures – both in construction and property development – was only 4.64 per cent in FY26. Gamuda's net profit margin for overseas ventures has been declining.
In FY22, Gamuda's overseas ventures returned 13.1 per cent. It then declined to 8.9 per cent in FY23, to 5.2 per cent in FY24 and FY25.
This shows that returns from Gamuda's large overseas ventures are getting thinner by the year.

Meanwhile, the group's orderbooks are heavy on overseas contracts. As of July 2026, Gamuda's unbilled orderbooks from overseas contracts stood at 57 per cent of the total, with Australian contracts making up 37 per cent of the total.
Since July 2026, Gamuda has secured a total RM8.2 billion worth of new contracts from Australia and RM2.7 billion from Taiwan.

In comparison, the group secured a RM1.7 billion hyperscale data centre job in Port Dickson and announced a joint venture with SD Guthrie Bhd and Gentari to develop a 680 MWac hybrid solar photovoltaic project with a battery energy storage system (BESS) in Perak.
These new contracts brought Gamuda's outstanding orderbook to RM62 billion.

"They argue that now the Malaysia orderbook is around 50 per cent vs Australia's which is around 30%. But the reality is the majority of new jobs will still come from Australia, and the margins are lowest among their operating geographical locations," says the analyst.

Beside overseas margins are usually lower than domestic, Gamuda's declining margin is also due to the profit recognition timing. At the moment, the existing contracts in Australia and Taiwan are at the early stage of execution.
An observer puts it that Gamuda is transitioning into heavier execution of the orderbook in FY27.

"As Gamuda's orderbook transitions into heavier execution, over 90 per cent of expected FY27 construction revenue is directly supported by existing contracts, driving projected construction revenue growth of 50 to 60 per cent this year, and a further around 20 per cent in FY28.
"Profitability will be further enhanced by a favourable project execution mix, high-margin property launches, and higher returns from its growing 6GW renewable energy portfolio," says the observer.

If Gamuda's construction revenue grew by 50 to 60 per cent in FY27, this means that it would reach between RM22.3 billion and RM23.8 billion, from RM14.9 billion in FY26. Assuming that net profit margins stays at five per cent, Gamuda could earn RM1.1 billion to RM1.2 billion.

That is not far off from the RM1.4 billion forecast net profit that the market is ascribing on the group. Another RM200 million to RM300 million of net profits could come from its property development segment.

Another risk factor is Gamuda's net gearing, which stood at more than the self-imposed 70 per cent ceiling as of end FY26. Total borrowings reached RM14.1 billion against RM4.7 billion of cash and marketable securities, leaving net debt of RM9.4 billion.

Short-term borrowings more than doubled to RM6.3 billion from a year ago, following land acquisitions in Vietnam and Singapore. Meanwhile, operating cash flow improved to RM808 million from a RM78 million outflow in FY25.

An observer said that Gamuda's rapid orderbook conversion, and bullet payments from the sold-out Eaton Park development in Vietnam, as well as expected cash inflows of RM5 billion over the next two years, will accelerate deleveraging from FY27 onwards.
The question now for Gamuda is execution, whether the group can actually grow its construction revenue by 50 to 60 per cent in FY27, or if the construction margins can start to recover.

In a note published on Sept 29, CGS International stated that Gamuda had raised its construction revenue projections for FY27 to FY28 which assumes a 30 per cent compound annualised growth rate (CAGR).

The 60 per cent year-on-year growth for FY27 assumes largely just its orderbook of RM61 billion, with minimal assumption of new wins. As of September, 91 per cent of the orderbook has yet to reach peak progress.
The orderbook is likely to stay at RM60 billion as of the end of the year, which is 20 per cent above target, said CGI International.
"This, together with better earnings delivery [with earnings per share (EPS) CAGR of 20 per cent between 2026 and 2028], could lead to a sustainable share price re-rating.

"We do not discount upside to FY27 forecast EPS given that three of its projects in New South Wales will be completed earlier than expected, where there is an incentive for early delivery," stated CGS International in the report.

1246df20968d1512: “Apa khabar?” “Khabar baik.” “Terima kasih.” “Sama-sama.”
These were among the basic Malay exchanges that home minister Saifuddin Nasution Ismail said foreign footballers learnt before their citizenship interviews.

“Adequate knowledge is subjective. Typically, for this category, our practice is that we coach them before the interview: ‘Apa khabar?’ (How are you?), they answer ‘Khabar baik’ (I am well). ‘Terima kasih’ (Thank you), they answer, ‘Sama-sama’ (You are welcome). That is the current practice,” he said.
“It does not say fluent, nor does it require in-depth knowledge. It says adequate. If they understand, we pass them,” he added, according to the New Straits Times.
Saifuddin is defending the level of Malay required by law, but the controversy over the seven players goes well beyond a language test.

Fifa found that falsified documents had been used in the naturalisation and eligibility process, while the Enforcement Agency Integrity Commission (EAIC) uncovered irregularities in the citizenship approvals.
The government must account for how officials handled the applications and assessed the supporting evidence.
Discretion needs limits

Saifuddin has acknowledged that some players did not meet the usual residency period for naturalisation. He argued that the Federal Constitution allowed him to count certain periods spent abroad as residence in Malaysia.
Article 19(3) sets the ordinary requirement at 10 years’ residence within the 12 years before an application, including the 12 months immediately before it.
The EAIC acknowledged the minister’s power to grant special approval under Article 19(2), read with Section 20(1)(e) of Part III of the Second Schedule to the Constitution.
It said the minister considered the players’ potential contribution to Malaysian football when exercising that discretion.
But the power to approve an application does not excuse a failure to follow proper procedures.
The EAIC found that officials considered the special approvals within an extremely short period and in an irregular manner.
It also flagged problems with entry permits, security screening, Malay language assessments and checks on the players’ renunciation of their original citizenship.

The commission urged the home ministry and national registration department (NRD) to review the applications and supporting documents. It also called for clearer guidelines on ministerial discretion and procedures for future cases.
The issue, then, is not simply whether Saifuddin had the power to approve the applications. It is whether officials properly scrutinised them before granting citizenship.
What did the authorities verify?
Saifuddin says the Football Association of Malaysia (FAM) must answer for the documents it submitted to Fifa to establish the players’ eligibility to represent Malaysia.
FAM must account for its submissions but its responsibility does not absolve the government of questions about the citizenship process.

Fifa found that falsified documents had been used to claim Malaysian family links for the players. The Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) upheld the finding of falsification. It restricted the players’ 12-month suspensions to official matches but retained the 350,000 Swiss franc fine against FAM.

The EAIC examined material from both the NRD and FAM and called for a review of the citizenship files. Its public findings do not specify that every document found to be forged went directly to the NRD. The authorities should clarify which documents they received and relied on.
That is central to the case. If doctored documents supported the citizenship applications, how did they pass the authorities’ checks?

The NRD had previously told Fifa that it checked documents relating to the players’ family lineage. Its director-general said officials could not retrieve the original handwritten birth records and issued copies based on secondary evidence.
The department should identify that evidence and explain how officials verified it.
The EAIC also flagged shortcomings in security screening, the Malay language test and checks on renunciation of foreign citizenship.

It noted that requirements concerning the surrender of foreign passports had not been met. As Malaysia does not recognise dual citizenship, the government should explain how officials dealt with these requirements in each case.
CAS did not rule on the legality of the citizenship grants under Malaysian law but that does not make the government’s handling of the applications any less deserving of scrutiny.
The falsification finding and the EAIC’s findings of irregularities demand a proper account of the decisions.
What about other applicants?
The controversy also raises questions about fairness to ordinary citizenship applicants.
Many wait years for a decision. Some have spent most or all of their lives in Malaysia. Their circumstances vary, and not everyone will qualify.
But the government should explain how it applies the law, assesses language proficiency, verifies documents and decides when special approval is justified.
Saifuddin can defend his constitutional powers. He cannot use those powers to sidestep questions about the evidence or the way officials handled the applications.
Nor can the government treat the FAM scandal as a matter for football authorities alone when the citizenship process raises its own concerns.
The language test may be satisfied by a few rehearsed exchanges. The larger test is whether the government can show that officials verified the evidence, followed the rules and applied them properly.
Citizenship is not a favour to be defended after the fact. It is a legal status that demands a credible process.
If the government stands by these approvals, it should produce the evidence that supports them and account for the irregularities the EAIC identified.
Until it does, the questions over how these seven players became Malaysians will remain.

40e2b05e2086e121: France's next political contest will also be a test of fiscal credibility. On 6 Oct, Marine Le Pen presented a programme promising €140 billion in spending cuts by 2032, net of at least €30 billion in tax cuts, according to Reuters. For a politician identified with national sovereignty, the message was revealing: political ambition now requires financial reassurance.

France has not defaulted. Its predicament is more gradual, but consequential. Successive governments have accumulated obligations that increasingly constrain their successors. The question is whether its political system can agree on an adjustment that investors will finance and citizens will accept.
The Cost of Political Delay

The European Commission's May 2026 assessment put France's public debt at 115.6 per cent of GDP in 2025 and its deficit at 5.1 per cent. It projected debt rising to 118.1 per cent in 2026 and 120.2 per cent in 2027. These projections are conditional, but their direction illustrates the challenge.

France's difficulties predate Le Pen's programme. Persistent deficits, weak growth and resistance to reforms have narrowed the government's choices. There is no painless combination of spending restraint, taxation and stronger growth. Delaying a settlement does not remove these choices; it can make them more expensive.

Borrowing costs require careful interpretation. French bond yields respond to eurozone interest-rate expectations and inflation, as well as domestic political risk. The gap between French and comparable German yields offers a clearer indication of relative market concern, although it is not a pure measure of fiscal credibility.

Nor do higher market yields immediately reprice the entire debt stock. Their effects accumulate as governments refinance maturing obligations and issue new debt. That gradual transmission gives policymakers time to respond. It also allows them to underestimate a burden that is still building.

France retains a diversified economy, substantial taxation capacity and deep financial markets. The danger is not that these strengths suddenly disappear. It is that interest payments absorb resources needed for investment, public services and protection against future shocks.

The fiscal task must therefore extend beyond cutting expenditure. Adjustment that damages productive investment or weakens growth can make the debt ratio harder to stabilise. Credibility depends on what is changed, how quickly, and whether the settlement can endure.
Le Pen's Credibility Test

Le Pen's announcement deserves scrutiny on precisely these terms. Its significance lies in the attempt to reconcile economic nationalism with fiscal restraint. A movement that promises to restore national control must also explain how it would finance the exercise of that control.

The announced savings remain political commitments. Their credibility depends on a transparent baseline, a realistic timetable and measures capable of surviving legal, administrative and parliamentary scrutiny.

Fraud prevention illustrates the difficulty. Recovering unpaid taxes is desirable, but anticipated recoveries cannot be treated as assured revenue. Administrative savings require decisions about staffing, services and responsibilities. Changes to France's financial relationship with the European Union involve obligations and negotiations, not simply unilateral announcements.

Tax reductions compound the challenge. A programme promising both lower taxation and substantial deficit reduction must explain which spending commitments will change and how essential services will be protected. Broad assurances about efficiency cannot settle those distributional questions.

The same standard should apply to every French party. Incumbents deserve no exemption because their language sounds reassuring; challengers deserve no presumption of competence because their promises are ambitious. Fiscal credibility must be demonstrated through coherent measures and plausible assumptions.

Giorgia Meloni's Italy offers a useful, limited comparison. Reuters' Breakingviews analysis argues that Le Pen faces a harder task in translating a nationalist platform into investor confidence, particularly given France's fragmented parliamentary landscape. The relevant lesson is the importance of governing capacity, rather than political branding.

Markets may welcome an announcement and subsequently reconsider it. Durable confidence requires evidence that a government can secure approval, implement its programme and sustain public consent. A favourable trading session cannot substitute for that work.
Sovereignty Has a Financing Cost

France's predicament exposes a tension within modern democracy. Voters authorise governments to make choices. Investors determine the terms on which they are prepared to finance borrowing. Neither source of influence eliminates the other.

Markets are not infallible arbiters of the public interest. They can exaggerate risks and react excessively to uncertainty. Nevertheless, a government that depends on continual borrowing cannot disregard the price investors demand.

Eurozone membership shapes France's options. Paris cannot independently set monetary policy or adjust a national exchange rate. It also benefits from a shared currency and common institutions. These arrangements provide support while limiting unilateral action; they do not remove the need for sustainable national budgets.

For Malaysia, the comparison is instructive without being exact. A national currency and monetary policy provide additional adjustment instruments. They do not guarantee greater fiscal space: inflation, exchange-rate pressures, debt composition and investor confidence still constrain policy. The lesson is to preserve flexibility through credible institutions and budgets, rather than assume that currency sovereignty makes borrowing constraints disappear.

France must also preserve the political legitimacy of adjustment. Citizens are more likely to accept difficult measures when burdens are distributed fairly, essential services remain credible and the government explains what its programme is intended to achieve.

Restoring confidence therefore requires more than persuading creditors that the accounts will improve. It requires persuading citizens that the adjustment will protect the country's capacity to prosper.

Political sovereignty supplies the authority to act. Fiscal credibility helps determine the room available to exercise it. France's challenge is to restore that room without sacrificing the social consent on which effective government depends.
Marine Le Pen may change the political conversation. She cannot repeal the arithmetic.

Economist Samirul Ariff Othman is an international relations analyst and a senior consultant with Global Asia Consulting (GAC). Samirul has a background as a senior researcher at the Malaysian Institute of Economic Research. The viewpoints articulated are solely those of the author.

c613770ab68d883f: KUALA LUMPUR: An accident can turn a worker's life upside down, with recovery often requiring more than medical treatment. Social Security Organisation (Perkeso) group chief executive officer Datuk Seri Dr Mohammed Azman Aziz Mohammed said its Lindung 24 Jam scheme provides eligible workers with access to treatment and rehabilitation following accidents occurring outside working hours.

Under its "Care Beyond Compensation" approach, eligible workers can receive rehabilitation equipment and injury-related implants, as well as physical rehabilitation at Perkeso's rehabilitation centres.

"This includes treatment at government hospitals or Perkeso panel hospitals, funding for rehabilitation equipment and injury-related implants, as well as physical rehabilitation at Perkeso-managed centres and access to vocational support to help workers return to their normal lives and jobs.
"This approach is important because the impact of an accident goes beyond medical bills, affecting income and the financial well-being of the worker's family," he told the New Straits Times.
Introduced on June 1, Lindung 24 Jam complements other Perkeso protections, with benefits subject to eligibility requirements and the nature of the injury.
Azman said a major challenge for workers involved in accidents was the possibility of disability that could affect their ability to work and disrupt their income.
"Typically, employers provide full wages for the first two months of medical leave, followed by half wages if the leave is extended into the third and fourth months.
"However, workers may no longer receive wages if they have to remain on medical leave from the fifth month onwards.
"Lindung 24 Jam helps ease this burden through the Temporary Disablement Benefit, which replaces income during approved medical leave.
"This helps ensure that workers' income is not disrupted when they suffer accidents outside working hours."
Under Section 52 of the Employees' Social Security Act, employers are also prohibited from dismissing or penalising workers while they receive Perkeso's Temporary Disablement Benefit.
If an injury results in permanent disability or death, other benefits are available, subject to the stipulated conditions.
These include Permanent Disablement Benefit, Dependants' Benefit and Funeral Benefit.
For workers who rely on daily wages, even a brief illness or injury can affect their ability to meet daily expenses and support their families.
Income replacement through the Temporary Disablement Benefit under the Employment Injury Scheme is therefore an important component of social protection.
Azman said personal insurance and Perkeso protection served different but complementary purposes.

While private medical insurance generally covers treatment according to the terms of the policy, Perkeso provides a broader social security safety net that can include income replacement, rehabilitation and long-term benefits, depending on the circumstances.

"Perkeso protection is not merely about cash payments when misfortune strikes. It covers treatment, rehabilitation, income replacement and long-term benefits, depending on the type of injury or circumstances.
"Having personal insurance does not necessarily mean a person no longer needs social security protection.
"The most important message is that accidents can happen at any time, anywhere and under any circumstances.
"Lindung 24 Jam was introduced to provide workers and their families with an additional layer of protection when unexpected risks arise," Azman said.

f33263fdee0f575a: MILAN: Milan police clashed on Sunday with protesters throwing stones and looting shops during demonstrations against poor services and the rising cost of living, a day after similar unrest in several Italian cities.

Police in riot gear fired tear gas and used water cannons after several hundred hooded protesters broke shop windows and set bins on fire in the area near central Piazza Duomo, sources with knowledge of the investigation told Reuters.
More than 60 protesters were taken to the police station for further checks, the sources added.
A total of 28 protesters were arrested after similar clashes erupted on Saturday in northern cities including Milan, Bologna, Brescia, Bergamo and Turin, according to a police report on Sunday.

The clashes had echoes of the violence in neighbouring France, where hundreds of thousands of people angered by rising costs and declining public services took to the streets on Saturday in some of the country's most violent protests in years.
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, facing an election next year, condemned the violence and announced a government meeting on Monday to discuss how to address the situation.
c308b663b5ed4464: KUALA LUMPUR: Perikatan Nasional will know this week whether it can use its logo in the upcoming Melaka polls, with the High Court here set to hear its application to stay the Registrar of Societies' (RoS) suspension order on Thursday.
The application is among four high-profile court cases scheduled for this week, including two related to the Negri Sembilan crisis and a defamation-related contempt action.
The High Court here had earlier allowed PN to proceed with a judicial review of two RoS notices but refused to suspend the order pending the outcome of the review.

PN is seeking to quash a suspension order dated Sept 23, issued under subsection 13(2A) of the Societies Act 1966. The order suspended all PN activities except those related to responding to a notice of intention to cancel its registration.
The other notice, dated Sept 22, proposed cancelling PN's registration and gave its chairman 30 days to make representations.
The outcome could have significant implications for the coalition, with the Melaka election scheduled for Nov 14.

Meanwhile, the Court of Appeal in Putrajaya will hold case management today for an appeal by Datuk Mubarak Dohak and five others against a July 8 High Court decision allowing Negri Sembilan's Dewan Keadilan dan Undang (DKU) and its secretary, Raja Norazli Raja Nordin, to initiate contempt proceedings against them over an alleged breach of a June 5 injunction.

On July 29, the appellate court granted an interim stay barring the Seremban High Court from proceeding with the contempt case. On Sept 7, it reserved its decision on the stay application.
The six include Mubarak, the disputed Undang Luak Sungai Ujong; Datuk Maarof Mat Rashad, the disputed Undang Luak Jelebu; and Datuk Abdul Rahim Yasin, the disputed Undang Luak Rembau.

The others are Johol Undang Datuk Muhammed Abdullah, Tunku Besar Tampin Tunku Syed Razman Tunku Syed Idrus Al-Qadri and Datuk Seri Badarudin Abdul Khalid, whom the DKU says was removed as Shahbandar Sungai Ujong on July 30.

The revocation was gazetted by order of Yang di-Pertuan Besar Tuanku Muhriz Tuanku Munawir, citing a breach of their pledge of allegiance.
The High Court will also hear a committal application today by entrepreneur Christy Ng and her company against J. Vikneshvra Rau, who operates the "archnionverse" Threads account.

The application stems from Vikneshvra's alleged failure to comply with a court order to publish a full-page apology in two major newspapers after a defamation suit over statements he posted last year.
9d251a345acbc2c1: KUALA LUMPUR: Over the past decade, more than 38,000 workers injured in accidents suffered a second blow when the Social Security Organisation (Perkeso) rejected their claims, classifying the incidents as non-employment related.

Deputy Human Resources Minister Datuk Khairul Firdaus Akbar Khan said the figure, recorded between 2015 and 2025, exposed a significant gap in social protection for workers injured outside working hours, particularly those without private insurance or takaful coverage.
The gap persisted in more recent years, with 12,306 claims rejected by Perkeso between 2023 and October last year because the injuries were classified as non-employment-related.
He said the figures highlighted the need for a broader safety net that protected workers beyond the workplace.

"Such a high number of cases required immediate intervention to ensure workers in Malaysia remained protected, not only during working hours but also outside working hours," he told the New Straits Times.

Khairul Firdaus said the issue was particularly pressing for B40 and some M40 workers, many of whom could not afford the monthly premiums for private insurance or takaful after prioritising basic household expenses.

Citing Bank Negara Malaysia data, he said personal insurance or takaful ownership among B40 workers remained low, at between four and 30 per cent, compared with 88 per cent among higher-income urban workers.
He said the introduction of the Lindung 24 Jam scheme on June 1 aimed to close the gap by extending social protection to non-employment accidents.
Under the scheme, workers contribute 0.75 per cent of their monthly wages. A worker earning RM1,500, for example, contributes about RM11.25 a month.
Khairul Firdaus said the low contribution could provide crucial support to workers who suffered serious injuries or disabilities from accidents outside working hours.

"When B40 or M40 workers suffer serious injuries or disabilities due to accidents outside working hours, they can lose their source of income and become exposed to financial risks that can severely affect their lives.
"Lindung 24 Jam helps close this gap by providing protection around the clock, including income replacement and benefits for dependents."
The scheme has already recorded a sharp increase in claims since its introduction.
Between June 1 and July 31, a total of 2,751 claims were submitted, averaging 45 a day.
Perkeso approved RM3.45 million in benefits for 2,508 recipients in July alone, bringing the total benefits paid during the first two months to RM4.69 million.
More than 90 per cent of claims were approved and processed within five days, Khairul Firdaus said.

The largest share of benefits went towards rehabilitation equipment and implants, amounting to RM3.69 million cumulatively, followed by more than RM909,800 in Temporary Disablement Benefits to replace income during medical leave.
Additionally, long-term benefits for dependants exceeded RM2 million.
Khairul Firdaus said more than half of Lindung 24 Jam beneficiaries after the first two months were lower-income workers earning below RM3,500 on average, while the remainder were from the M40 group.
He said most beneficiaries were workers involved in everyday accidents outside working hours.
The figures, he said, showed that accidents outside working hours were not isolated incidents but a recurring financial risk for workers and their families.
Khairul Firdaus added that Lindung 24 Jam should not be viewed as a substitute for private insurance, but as a complementary layer of protection.

He said private medical cards were generally designed to cover hospital treatment, while Perkeso protection provided income replacement and longer-term support in cases of permanent disability or death.

Among the benefits available under Lindung 24 Jam are Temporary Disablement Benefit, Permanent Disablement Benefit, Dependants' Benefit, Constant Attendance Allowance of RM500 a month, funeral benefits and rehabilitation services through Perkeso facilities.
"Private insurance and Perkeso protection do not overlap. Instead, they complement each other," Khairul Firdaus said.
He added that the scheme was ultimately based on the principle of social solidarity, where contributions help spread financial risks across the workforce.

fb34ed50cef3bed0: "From this point forward, all of United States documents and hopefully the world's will be changed to use the much more accurate term 'super' as opposed to artificial." That was Donald Trump at the United Nations General Assembly on Sept 22, and true to form, he didn't stop at a soundbite.

A week later, he signed an executive order titled "Inaugurating the Era of Super Intelligence", ordering federal agencies to swap "artificial intelligence" and "AI" for "super intelligence" and "SI" across official documents and websites. The same day, executives from Meta, Nvidia, Google, OpenAI, xAI and Anthropic signed a separate, voluntary White House Accord on Super Intelligence.
It's tempting to laugh this off as branding, especially since Trump's own explanation was that "artificial" "makes intelligence sound fake. It is not fake." But wait a minute.

Words matter, and this one has a specific meaning. The term was popularised by philosopher Nick Bostrom, then at the University of Oxford, in his 2014 book Superintelligence, and it describes not a machine that matches us but one that vastly outperforms the brightest humans in practically every field.

Today's systems aren't there yet, and Trump may simply think "artificial" sounds cheap. But when Meta has had a division literally called Meta Superintelligence Labs since 2025 and the world's most powerful government adopts the same vocabulary, I can't help but feel they are preparing us for something far beyond today's chatbots.
So what does that world look like? Three questions keep nagging at me.
Do we still need schools?

Six years ago, I argued in this column that AI could help fix our broken school system, pointing to Chinese and American platforms that taught maths at each student's own pace. The evidence has since piled up faster than I expected.

In 2025, the World Bank published the results of a six-week after-school programme in Nigeria's Edo State, where students worked in pairs with Microsoft Copilot, a GPT-4-powered assistant, in up to two 90-minute sessions a week under a teacher's supervision. The gains, the lead researchers later wrote, "correspond to nearly 1.5 years of typical learning in just six weeks", outperforming around 80% of the education programmes tested in randomised trials across the developing world.

Now imagine that this tutor isn't merely good but superintelligent and available to every child in every kampung at any hour. The classroom as a place where a teacher pours the same facts into a roomful of young heads at the same speed and we simply can't compete with that.

But schools will survive, because they'll become the place where children learn what no machine can learn on their behalf: how to make friends, lose gracefully, argue without hating and work alongside people who aren't like them. As I wrote back then, the secret ingredient is EQ, or emotional intelligence, and a superintelligent tutor only makes it more precious.
Why would we even work?

In 1930, the British economist John Maynard Keynes predicted that within a century we would be so much richer that "three-hour shifts or a fifteen-hour week" might be all the work we would need. We are four years from his deadline, and Malaysian law still sets the normal working week at up to 45 hours, three times what he imagined.

Elon Musk, never one for understatement, thinks the machines will finally deliver on that promise. "In a benign scenario, probably none of us will have a job," he told the VivaTech conference in Paris in 2024, with what he called "universal high income" taking the place of wages.
I'm not going to pretend that's guaranteed, since whether superintelligence brings abundance for all or riches for a few depends on who owns the machines.

But if we get it right, Keynes already told us what our real challenge would be: "how to use his freedom from pressing economic cares, how to occupy the leisure, which science and compound interest did for him, to live wisely and agreeably and well." Work won't vanish so much as become something we choose, like a Sunday evening game of futsal.
What does a world of superintelligent humanoids look like?
Years ago, I toured a factory outside Shenzhen that was frantic with activity yet almost void of human life. Those were single-purpose machines, impressive but hardly intelligent.

Today's humanoids are something else entirely. In July 2025, China's Unitree priced its R1 humanoid at 39,900 yuan, about RM24,000, while Musk has said Tesla's Optimus could eventually cost RM82,000 to RM123,000 once it's mass-produced.

Investment bank Morgan Stanley expects close to a billion humanoids in use by 2050, mostly in industry and commerce. Put a superintelligent mind inside each of those bodies and the list of "AI-proof" jobs I published in this column in 2020, from construction worker and mechanic to nurse and caregiver, goes straight into the bin.

Picture a machine that harvests paddy in Kedah at dawn, rewires your house by noon and sits with your ageing parents through the night, never tired and never impatient. That isn't a dystopia. It's the end of drudgery.

Whatever Trump's reasons for choosing the name, the industry he's naming has made no secret of where it's heading. Keynes addressed his essay to "our grandchildren" - the generation that would first have to decide what to do with all that freedom, and it turns out those grandchildren are us – or at least the younger ones among us.

730492500c4d9ed9: Beberapa hari kini masih lagi terngiang-ngiang soalan berani seorang mahasiswa wanita daripada Universiti Malaya kepada Khairy Jamaluddin dan Onn Hafiz Ghazi, menteri besar Johor. Backlash atau tindakan balas terhadap mahasiswa tersebut daripada orang Melayu memang saya sudah jangkakan. Saya dah biasa dengan backlash sedemikian. Bila kita orang Melayu hendak menasihati orang Melayu memang ini padahnya. Namun demikian, dalam artikel ini saya hendak mengajukan empat soalan tentang isu ini yang perlu direnungi oleh kita semua. Saya tidak tahulah sama ada orang Melayu boleh berubah atau tidak, minat nak berubah atau tidak ataupun mereka rasa kaum mereka telah pun sempurna dan hanya orang lain perlu berubah. Apa-apa pun jawapannya saya tanya jugalah soalan-soalan saya.

Soalan pertama saya adalah berkait dengan kenapa KJ kembali ke Umno? Kalau jawapan beliau kepada mahasiswa itu nampak macam suatu yang berprinsip dan bermoral, kenapa beliau kembali menjadi ahli Umno, despite knowing pasal isu pemgampunan dan kes rasuah yang sejelas-jelasnya dibuktikan di mahkamah? KJ adalah seorang yang cukup hebat. Beliau kena campak daripada Umno tetapi menjadi lebih penting dan lebih dipercayai dan diyakini semua golongan masyarakat setelah dibuang. Daripada seorang ‘menantu PM’ KJ berupaya membuat reinvention sebagai seorang personaliti media yang paling popular. Bagaimanakah seorang yang bergelumang dengan parti seperti Umno dan menjadi figura kontroversial sebagai ketua Pemuda Umno boleh pusing 180 darjah menjadi personaliti yang ada ‘kredibiliti’ di kaca mata semua rakyat termasuk merentas jurang kaum?

That is something incredible yang saya tidak pernah lihat. Berbanding dengan populariti Rafizi Ramli, KJ menang hands down. Rafizi hanya seorang one dimensional politician tetapi KJ memperlihatkan sifat multi-dimensional yang cukup mengagumkan. Tetapi, saya tahu yang beliau sebenarnya tidak pernah berubah langsung dan terbukti apabila beliau kembali ke pangkuan Umno kenyataan-kenyataannya sudah menjadi perangai Umno yang lama. Kenapakah KJ tidak menyahut seruan rakannya Ong Kian Ming untuk membuka wadah baharu politik? Saya kira kata ‘orang putih’ memang benarlah a leopard never changes its spots.

Soalan kedua saya pula adalah kepada Onn Hafiz. Beliau telah menjawab soalan mahasiswa tersebut dengan suatu syarat iaitu semua pendakwaan rasuah jangan ada sifat pendakwaan terpilih atau selective prosecution. Saya hendak bertanya soalan kepada Onn, adakah kes Najib Razak itu suatu selective prosecution? Kita semua boleh mengikuti the money trail dalam kes SRC dan juga 1MDB. Bukan seperti kes Anwar Ibrahim dulu dengan perubahan tarikh, tempat serta forced confession dua saksi dan macam-macam kerenah yang membuatkan sesiapa mengikuti kes tersebut tidak yakin langsung terhadap pertuduhan dan penghukuman.

Sekarang kita ada RCI Tabung Haji dan pendakwaan pun sedang dijalankan. Kejap nanti kes Felda, Mara dan entah berapa banyak kes lagi. Dalam RCI kita semua jelas mengikuti kenyataan penyiasatan yang terperinci maka apakah yang dimaksudkan oleh Onn tentang selective prosecution itu kita sukar nak pastikan.

Soalan ketiga saya adalah secara umum kepada sesiapa yang seperti Ummi Umairah Bakhit yang cuba dengan ikhlas untuk menegur atau menasihati orang Melayu. Saya telah masak dalam isu ini sebab saya pun telah dapat banyak backlash setelah lebih 10 tahun cuba untuk memperbaiki kaum saya sendiri.

Jelas, dalam pengalaman saya, Melayu yang hendak sokong tidak akan terkata apa-apa secara terbuka sekadar hantar WhatsApp sahaja. Tetapi, Melayu yang tidak bersetuju akan banyak memberi bidasan walaupun tak ada logik dan tak ada perbahasan yang munasabah. Di mana tokoh-tokoh Melayu bukan politik yang bakal menyokong Ummi? Memang tidak akan menjelma dalam kalangan ahli agama, profesor atau tokoh korporat yang berwibawa. She will be alone. Tetapi, kalau ada ahli politik Melayu yang mengecam bukan Melayu, maka ramailah yang akan keluar menjadi hulubalang bangsa. Saya kasihan kepada Ummi yang beranggapan Melayu yang cerdik pandai akan banyak menyokongnya dengan lantang. It will not happen, I am afraid.

Soalan keempat saya adalah implikasi masa depan Melayu. Kita telah melihat kemenangan besar PAS dan Umno di Johor dan Negeri Sembilan. Jangkaan mudah Melaka pun akan dimenangi secara besar oleh PAS dan Umno akan membuktikan penolakan terhadap sindiran Ummi tentang parti politik Melayu dan rasuah. Saya telah pun menulis dengan jelas pandangan akademik saya bahawa Melayu ramai yang tidak kisah tentang rasuah dan itu pun banyak dapat backlash.

effd5dc5dc1f9ab2: PETALING JAYA: Splitting a purchase into several smaller payments can make almost any expenditure feel more manageable. For younger Malaysians in particular, buy now, pay later (BNPL) has clearly become part of everyday spending.

According to a written reply by the finance ministry recently published on the Parliament website, Malaysians aged 30 and below made 65.9 million BNPL transactions worth RM5.4 billion during the first six months of the year. This accounted for 37.9% of all BNPL transactions in the country and 36.7% of their total value.

Across all age groups, Malaysians made 173.9 million BNPL transactions worth RM14.7 billion over that period. The sheer volume illustrates how rapidly an instalment-payment option once associated mainly with online shopping has moved into mainstream consumer spending.

BNPL typically allows shoppers to receive a product or service immediately while spreading payment over a number of instalments. According to the Consumer Credit Commission, such schemes are now commonly used not just online but at physical retailers, particularly for food and beverages, retail shopping, transport and other services.

That convenience is a large part of the appeal, especially for consumers who would rather divide a purchase into smaller amounts than pay the full price upfront. But several separate commitments can also be harder to keep track of when each instalment looks relatively modest on its own.

The latest figures show that, as of June 30, young users had RM2.4 billion in outstanding BNPL financing. Of that, RM96.8 million was classified as non-performing, equivalent to 4% of their outstanding balance.

Those numbers need some perspective, however. The finance ministry said earlier this year that BNPL debt represented only around 0.3% of Malaysia’s overall household debt, while Bank Negara has similarly described the segment as small in relation to total household borrowing, even as its rapid expansion warrants continued monitoring.
BNPL use has grown quickly: the finance ministry reported in July that active BNPL account holders had reached eight million in the first quarter of 2026, up from 7.5 million at the end of 2025.

That expansion has prompted tighter regulation. The Consumer Credit Act 2025 came into force on March 1, bringing previously unregulated non-bank credit activities, including BNPL schemes, under the supervision of the Consumer Credit Commission.

Under new conduct standards, providers are required to follow rules on disclosure, fees, affordability, debt collection and assistance for consumers facing financial difficulty. The commission also requires an affordability assessment when a BNPL user is given a credit limit above RM1,000, while allowing providers to set lower thresholds for groups considered more vulnerable.

Additionally, BNPL companies are being brought into a licensing framework, with existing providers given a transition period to comply with the new requirements. The aim, according to the commission, is to encourage more transparent and responsible credit practices.

The newest figures do not show that young Malaysians are generally overspending or unable to manage their commitments. They do, however, demonstrate how significant BNPL has become in the spending habits of people aged 30 and below.

That distinction matters because BNPL can feel different from taking out a conventional loan or using a credit card, particularly when there is little to no interest attached to a purchase. Yet it still creates a future payment obligation, and several small instalments across different purchases can add up.

For young consumers, the appeal is easy to understand: BNPL offers flexibility at the checkout and can make larger purchases easier to manage. The RM5.4 billion spent in six months shows, however, that those small instalments now represent a very large slice of Malaysia’s consumer-credit landscape.
bde3df7402a8dc14: LONDON: Arsenal ground out a 1-0 win at Nottingham Forest to stay in touch with pacesetters Manchester City as Manchester United's winless run in the Premier League stretched to five games.
Chelsea and Liverpool are in the top five after victories, while free-scoring Brighton dazzled in a 5-0 mauling of fierce rivals Crystal Palace that leaves them third in the table.
AFP Sport looks at three talking points from the weekend action:
Arteta's bench power
Mikel Arteta stood with his arms folded and a look of intense frustration as Arsenal laboured to break down stubborn Nottingham Forest on Sunday.
The champions had failed to muster a shot on target in the first 70 minutes of a league game for the first time since 2023, and Arteta was beginning to lose his patience.
But the Gunners boss has powerful weapons on the substitutes' bench and he made full use of his resources to turn the tide by the banks of the River Trent.
Arteta sent on Noni Madueke for the underwhelming Eberechi Eze at half-time and introduced Mikel Merino, Viktor Gyokeres and Jurrien Timber as the second half wore on.
Madueke was the key to victory, cutting in from the left flank to unleash a powerful drive that deflected past Forest keeper Matz Sels in the 80th minute.
That was enough for second-placed Arsenal to secure a sixth win from seven league games and close to within three points of leaders Manchester City.
"If you look at the quality of our starting XI and bench, it's absurd, so we know that we're going to start some and finish some," said Madueke.
Carrick fails to ease pressure
Manchester United manager Michael Carrick took the positives from his team's 1-1 draw at Leeds but he must be wondering where the next win is coming from.
The Old Trafford club now have just two victories in 10 matches in all competitions this season after Dominic Calvert-Lewin cancelled out Bryan Mbeumo's first-half opener at Elland Road.
The build-up to Sunday's game was dominated by chatter over Lisandro Martinez's explosive interview in midweek, when he took aim at club chiefs for a lack of investment in the squad.
United showed fight but looked short of firepower and a cutting edge -- the good vibes of last season, when Carrick's men finished third in the Premier League, have vanished.
The Red Devils, in 13th spot, have their fewest wins at this stage of a top-flight campaign since 1986/87.
Carrick's job does not appear under immediate threat but, with daunting trips to Chelsea and Liverpool coming up, the fanbase is growing restive.
Record-breaker Maresca
History-making Manchester City manager Enzo Maresca appears unfazed by the threat of punishment hanging over the club after it was found guilty of multiple breaches of Premier League financial rules.
City's 3-2 home win over Ipswich on Saturday made Maresca the first manager in Premier League history to win his opening seven league games in charge of a club.
The list of those who have had six straight wins includes his celebrated City predecessor Pep Guardiola, who achieved the feat in the 2016/17 season.
Erling Haaland scored twice at the Etihad to take his overall tally in all competitions to 12 this season while Phil Foden scored his first goal of the campaign.
Maresca said he was happy to see his players improving.
"We give credit to the players... they are not worried about people who judge from outside," he said.

0f582c1904e88fe1: KUALA LUMPUR: With less than two weeks before nomination day for the Melaka election, the battle lines are taking shape as Barisan Nasional, Pas and Pakatan Harapan signal their readiness to contest.
But despite preparations being well underway, uncertainty over political cooperation and seat negotiations means the final electoral landscape may not be clear until nomination day.
BN and Pas have indicated that their candidate lists are ready, while PH has finalised seat allocations among its components, PKR, DAP and Amanah.
The question now is whether the parties will stick to their respective plans or strike last-minute deals to avoid multi-cornered contests.

Universiti Malaya political analyst Dr Mohammad Tawfik Yaakub said early candidate preparations demonstrated organisational readiness and allowed parties to assess candidates' acceptance among voters.
"Announcing candidate lists is not merely about who will contest. It is also closely linked to seat negotiations and political cooperation.
"The real challenge is ensuring that seat allocations are accepted by the parties and their supporters," he told the New Straits Times.
Tawfik said BN held a clear advantage as the incumbent government, backed by its established grassroots network and election machinery.
Having won 21 of Melaka's 28 state seats in 2021, BN is seeking to defend its majority under caretaker Chief Minister Datuk Seri Ab Rauf Yusoh.
Tawfik believes a proposed BN-plus arrangement involving Pas could further strengthen the coalition's prospects.
"I expect BN-plus, with Pas contesting under the BN symbol, to win at least 24 seats, including three additional seats in Bemban, Sungai Udang and Bukit Katil."
However, Universiti Islam Antarabangsa Malaysia political scientist Dr Syaza Shukri said the political landscape remained fragmented, with parties seemingly preparing to contest independently.
"There are still many unanswered questions. We may have to wait until nomination day to see how political cooperation takes shape."
Syaza said BN and Perikatan Nasional currently appeared to have an advantage over PH, but questioned whether BN could increase its seat tally.
"I don't think BN can win more seats. In 2021, it won several constituencies by narrow margins. BN's strength in Melaka is not as dominant as in Johor."
She added that even cooperation between BN and PN might not increase BN's tally if some constituencies had to be allocated to its partners.
For Rauf, the election will also test whether his administration's grassroots engagement can translate into electoral support.

His "Wakil Rakyat Untuk Rakyat" programme, aimed at engaging the public, has covered all 28 constituencies, attracting more than 100,000 participants and recording 5,170 complaints for follow-up action.
Rauf has cited an 80 per cent approval rate for the initiative.
Meanwhile, PH faces the challenge of defending its five seats, while Bersatu's prospects could be affected if Pas reaches an agreement with BN.
Tawfik cautioned that poorly coordinated seat arrangements could lead to multi-cornered contests and split votes.
He said candidate acceptance, grassroots machinery, local issues and voter turnout would be key to the election outcome.
For now, the parties may have their candidates ready, but Melaka's battle lines remain unsettled.
Whether BN can defend or expand its majority will depend on the alliances forged, candidates fielded and their ability to turn grassroots support into votes.
