c11ae2200e25ab7e: GLASGOW: Celtic crushed title rivals Hearts 7-1 as the Scottish Premiership leaders moved four points clear at the top with a statement victory on Sunday.
Martin O'Neill's side scored five times in a scintillating first half display at Parkhead.
Kieran Tierney and Benjamin Nygren struck in the opening 10 minutes before Callum Osmand bagged a brace as Celtic punished Hearts' poor defending.
Laurent Mendy pulled one back for Hearts but Jamie McCart's own goal was followed by second half strikes by Camilo Duran and Nygren.
After second-placed Rangers were held to a 2-2 draw by Dundee on Saturday, Celtic seized control of the title race with their eighth win from nine league games.
Third-placed Hearts are eight points adrift of Celtic following a painful return to the scene of one of the most bitter experiences in the club's history.

Hearts failed miserably in their bid for a small measure of revenge over Celtic in the first meeting between the clubs since the Hoops beat the Edinburgh team to the title with a 3-1 win over them on the final day of last season.
That loss denied Hearts a first title since 1960 and extended the duopoly of Celtic and Rangers as Scotland's only two champions in the last 41 years.
Handing Hearts only their second defeat in 14 games in all competitions was a welcome boost for Celtic after the east end of Glasgow was engulfed by crisis talk in recent weeks.
Thursday's 4-1 Europa League defeat by Benfica condemned Celtic to a fourth loss in their last five matches, while O'Neill reportedly considered quitting only a couple of weeks ago.
A section of Celtic's fan-base are furious with the club's hierarchy over their perceived failure to spend enough to establish the team as Champions League regulars.
Yet Celtic took just six minutes to ease the pre-match tension as Liam Scales flicked on Mika Baur's corner and Tierney pounced to head home from close-range.

O'Neill hired Ross Grant from Hearts to be his new set-piece coach in the summer and the move appeared to be a masterstroke after Celtic doubled their lead from another corner as Nygren's deflected volley flashed past Hearts goalkeeper Beau Reus.
Osmand intercepted Sabri Guendouz's woeful pass in the 36th minute and finished with aplomb.
Hearts were in disarray and Osmand marked his first start for Celtic with another goal in the 38th minute with a close-range header.
Mendy reduced the deficit in the 41st minute with a ferocious blast from just inside the area.
But rampant Celtic made it five in the closing seconds of a remarkable half as Stephen Kingsley diverted Baur's shot into his own net off McCart.
Duran notched the sixth in the 49th minute, slotting past Reus, and Nygren converted Kasper Hogh's pass in the 83rd minute to complete Hearts' humiliation.
5eeb24997162d18a: SOFIA: A bomb threat against an Austrian Airlines flight from Tel Aviv to Vienna on Sunday forced the plane to divert to Bulgaria, according to Bulgarian authorities and the airline.

c948bd483244c15f: BRIGHTON: Brighton manager Fabian Hurzeler praised the inspirational Diego Gomez after his goal from the halfway line set the stage for a 5-0 thrashing of Crystal Palace in the Premier League on Sunday.

KUALA LUMPUR: The MediAsas Plan scheme, set to launch in January 2027, will provide a financial and healthcare safety net for Malaysia's middle-income group (M40), who are currently facing medical inflation.

5e351572ec5bae2d: PARIS: President Emmanuel Macron on Sunday slammed the "unbridled" violence that erupted in cost-of-living protests across France, as police battled protesters and looters in new clashes in Paris.

Nearly 2,400 people were arrested Saturday in unrest that represented some of the worst urban violence in France in years, with almost 1,000 police and gendarmes injured, seven seriously, the interior ministry said.

In an address to the nation, Macron said local authorities would be able to ban – "if necessary" – certain rallies in coming days. But he stopped short of announcing drastic measures, such as a state of emergency or curfew.
"Tonight, we all feel anger and shame," Macron said of the devastation brought by the protests that include town halls burned down and hundreds of businesses looted or damaged.

"Looking at these images, we all asked ourselves: what is going through their minds? How can French people do this to France?" said Macron, who insisted there must be a distinction between protesters with "legitimate demands" and "those who destroyed, smashed, and looted."
He vowed the authorities would be "uncompromising" towards the "agitators from ultra-left fringe groups, joined by numerous delinquents" who "unleashed unbridled violence in our cities."

AFP journalists said police Sunday fired tear gas and stun grenades at hundreds of people gathered in a Paris square following social media calls for a gathering that authorities said had not been approved.
Bottles and rocks were hurled at police who made 42 arrests, according to authorities. At least five stores were looted around Republique square.
Other stores in central Paris also had windows smashed and the city hall told many to close. In the southeastern city of Lyon, police battled youths who attempted to loot a luxury clothing store.

The unrest came just months before a presidential election where centrist Macron cannot stand again and Marine Le Pen, the far-right presidential candidate for the National Rally party, is riding high in the polls.

With images of French town halls burning and shops being looted grabbing headlines around the world, US President Donald Trump waded into the debate, blaming immigration for the unrest.
"France is burning! The immigration of people from an entirely different world, people with hatred in their hearts, has shattered that once great country," Trump said in a social media post.
- 'ALL NECESSARY LESSONS' -
Macron vowed that top officials would "make decisions in coordination with mayors to protect our cities, public buildings, and businesses."

Some opposition politicians have already called for the sacking of Interior Minister Laurent Nunez.
Macron said he had asked Nunez to "draw all necessary lessons", particularly with regard to intelligence gathering and anticipation, adding he expected "clear answers."
"It's like we had a war," a 78-year-old Paris resident Mehmet Ozeden told AFP amid burnt street barricades from Saturday's protests.
The city of Limoges lost its 19th-century town hall to a fire that local prefect, Maurice Barate, told news channel LCI had been deliberately set by "a wild horde."
In Lyon, a tourist office in the city centre was set ablaze during the protests amid multiple clashes and looting.
A 17-year-old boy had his right hand blown off by a crowd-control grenade in the southern city of Saint-Etienne. In Mulhouse a 17-year-old girl lost an eye, according to prosecutors. --AFP

2074fe3cf694754c: NOTTINGHAM: Mikel Arteta said Arsenal's strength in depth will be key to their Premier League title defence after Noni Madueke came off the bench to clinch a 1-0 win against Nottingham Forest on Sunday.
Arteta's side were well below their best at the City Ground and did not register a shot on target until Madueke bagged their winner 10 minutes from full-time.
While the Gunners earned few style points in the east midlands, they will not be overly concerned after moving within three points of leaders Manchester City.
Arteta is able to dip into one of the stronger substitutes' benches in the top-flight and he made full use of the resources at his disposal to turn the tide by the banks of the River Trent.
Crucially, he sent on Madueke for the underwhelming Eberechi Eze at half-time.
He also introduced Mikel Merino, Viktor Gyokeres and Jurrien Timber as the second half wore on.
It was Madueke who provided the key intervention, cutting in from the left flank to unleash a powerful drive that deflected past Forest keeper Matz Sels in the 80th minute.
"We had to earn it until the last second. They are a well coached team and hard to break down. We had to take risks, they are a dangerous team," Arteta said.
"We had to manage the emotional part really well. We stayed focused and the finishers made a huge impact."
Arsenal are in the midst of a hectic schedule which included a Champions League win over Lille in midweek and a looming European trip to Bayern Munich on Wednesday.
Arteta's ability to rest key players without significantly weakening his team could be a major factor in the title race.
"Some of them played three days ago and some of them will start the next game and they know that everyone has to be at it," he said.
"If you are needed after 60 minutes, 45 minutes and sometimes two minutes. We have a squad now that can deliver in moments and we have to use that.
"Noni, Jurrien, Mikel was brilliant when he came on and Viktor really changed the game, all of them did and that's what we need.
"Noni obviously the highlight because he scored the goal and that's the difference."
After a shock 3-0 loss at Brighton on September 19, second-placed Arsenal have bounced back with three successive victories.
The north Londoners have not been able to recapture the relentless consistency that took them to a first title in 22 years last season.
But they retain the priceless ability to grind out wins and this was their sixth in seven league matches.
"Sometimes you can get frustrated with teams who are difficult to break down. First half we didn't have a shot on target and that's something we discussed," Arteta said.
"We had another two big ones in the second half but the only one on target we had was a little deflection and it's in."--AFP

TOKYO: Japanese scientists are readying a mission to Mars's moons to retrieve samples that could help unlock the origins of the Solar System and life on Earth, in what aims to be the first round trip to the Martian region.

The unmanned Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) probe, a collaboration with US and European space agencies as well as numerous universities and tech companies, could also help lay the groundwork for eventual human exploration.
The flagship H3 rocket carrying the MMX is set to blast off from the Tanegashima Space Centre on Tuesday at 4.41am, according to the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA).
The spacecraft will arrive near Mars one year later, where it will orbit its moon Phobos for up to three years before landing and collecting at least 10 grams of material from the surface.
A rover dubbed IDEFIX — the French name for the comic hero Asterix's dog — will first conduct surface observations aimed at ensuring a safe landing.
"The sampling (from) Phobos is of course the world's first, but it means... this is the first round trip to the Martian system," MMX project manager Yasuhiro Kawakatsu said.

JAXA said the mission will also explore the possibility of using Phobos as a "natural space station" by establishing the requirements for a round trip to Mars — something "essential for crewed Mars exploration".
It will also observe the Red Planet's moon Deimos, although it will not land on it, before returning to Earth.

"MMX will shed light on the transport mechanisms that delivered water, volatiles, and organic compounds from the outer Solar System to the inner rocky planet region – processes that may have played a key role in making these worlds habitable," said Patrick Michel, a French astrophysicist working on IDEFIX.

"If Phobos and Deimos are indeed remnants of these early delivery systems, they may hold clues to the origins of life itself, or, to be more correct, to the transport of the materials that were key to the emergence of life on rocky planets."
MMX is a collaboration with France's National Centre for Space Studies, the German Aerospace Centre, NASA, the European Space Agency and about 20 universities and tech companies. — AFP
42aa0a6282c217c2: LONDON: Arsenal struck late to beat Nottingham Forest and keep the pressure on Premier League leaders Manchester City on Sunday, while struggling Manchester United dropped more points in a draw at Leeds.

Argentina centre-back Martinez gave an explosive interview in Spain on Tuesday during which he criticised the lack of investment in the summer transfer window.
Carrick insisted on Friday that United had "moved on" from the incident and Martinez was named in the starting line-up.

Mbeumo, playing as United's target man, wasted a couple of chances but broke the deadlock in the 35th minute when he guided a Youri Tielemans cross into the bottom corner for his fourth goal of the season.

Leeds put the visitors under sustained pressure after the break and were level in the 51st minute when England forward Calvert-Lewin controlled the ball on his chest and finished at full stretch after Tarik Muharemovic's header from a corner.

Only three sides in Premier League history have scored more goals in their first seven games of a season than Brighton's haul of 23.

CANADA will not allow medically assisted suicide for people whose only condition is mental illness, its justice minister said, seeking to close debate on one of the country's most controversial healthcare issues.

Canada legalised assisted dying for those at the end of life in 2016. The right was extended to those suffering from serious and incurable illnesses in 2021, even if death was not "reasonably foreseeable".

Initially, Canada was to allow assisted death regardless of condition by 2024, but that date was pushed back three years, with the government saying it wanted to make sure the already overwhelmed mental health system was ready.
Without government action, people exclusively suffering from a mental illness would have had access to assisted suicide in March, when the exclusion was set to expire.

But Justice Minister Sean Fraser said recently that Canada's Liberal government plans to pass legislation that will prohibit assisted suicide for people whose only underlying medical condition is mental illness.
"Canada has made a decision not to move forward with the expansion (of assisted suicide).
"While there is not a perfect consensus on this issue, we believe this is the correct approach."
Fraser's announcement follows recommendations from an advisory panel which in June urged the government not to expand assisted suicide rights.
That panel raised concerns about the lack of mental health support in communities across the country and the risk that suffering patients would choose death because they could not access care.
The committee also highlighted debate among mental health experts as to whether mental illness could ever be deemed incurable.

A majority of Canadians support the right to assisted suicide, but in recent months some medical professionals have called for a review of the policy, including how patients receive approval to end their lives. — AFP
153d7aa71e1d0ae1: BEIJING: China's economic growth is expected to again miss its official target on Monday, dragged down by a global energy shock and slumping domestic demand, with surging exports the only bright spot.
The world's second-largest economy has charted a diverging path in recent years – an AI-fuelled export boom is masking the impact of a persistent real estate crisis and gloomy consumer sentiment.
Beijing is hoping for an annual growth this year of 4.5% to 5%, its lowest goal in decades.
But an AFP poll of economists suggests growth fell just below that range from July to September at 4.4% – still a slight improvement from the second quarter's 4.3%.
"Exports seem to be the only outperformer," Guo Shan of Hutong Research told AFP.
She said China risked missing its official target for the year, spurring a recent roll-out of mortgage subsidies for certain home purchases and support for infrastructure investment.
Beijing "will need to work faster to deploy the funds so as to hit the growth target," she added.
The Chinese economy is also under pressure from the spiking cost of energy caused by the US war with Iran, which has stymied shipping from the oil-rich Gulf.
China is the world's largest importer of crude oil.

Higher crude prices and "protracted uncertainty and structural headwinds" led the International Monetary Fund to last week slightly downgrade its projection for China's annual growth this year to 4.5%.
IMF officials gathering in Bangkok for the fund's meetings with the World Bank described Beijing's recent support measures as "limited".
'Rebalancing' needed

Economists say that China's economy must shift towards a more sustainable growth model powered more by domestic consumption than traditional drivers like construction, property development and exports.
That long-awaited "rebalancing" of the Chinese economy has yet to materialise, IMF Asia and Pacific department director Krishna Srinivasan said.
Exports – for decades the engine of China's economy – remain a bright spot.
Official data released last week showed that China's overseas shipments were on course for another record trade surplus after reaching US$1.2 trillion last year.
That export boom has been underpinned in large part by insatiable global demand for AI-related products including computers, semiconductors and data centre equipment.
But elsewhere, China's soaring surpluses are increasingly stoking tensions with key trading partners, including the EU and the US.
Talks this month between EU trade chief Maros Sefcovic and Chinese counterpart Wang Wentao ended with an agreement to limit exports of Chinese hybrid vehicles to Europe.
Many critics contend that Beijing's extensive subsidies doled out in recent years to domestic industries have given them an unfair advantage in foreign markets.
Domestic demand woes have also exacerbated the problem, as manufacturers increasingly look overseas for new growth.

LONDON: Liverpool bounced back from last week's 3-0 Premier League drubbing by Manchester City with a workmanlike 2-1 win at Brentford on Saturday, as winger Bradley Barcola showcased the full range of his talents despite spurning two gilt-edged chances.

Keane Lewis-Potter had given the home side the lead in the 44th minute but Yehor Yarmoliuk was sent off for an attempted headbutt deep into first-half stoppage time, and Victor Munoz and Alexander Isak completed Liverpool's comeback with second-half goals to seal the three points.

"Super-happy with the win. It's a tough ground, it's a tough team to play, especially away from home. We knew it was going to be a bit of a scrappy game and it's important to come out on top," Isak said.

Vitaly Janelt picked up a second yellow card in stoppage time to leave Brentford with nine men, and Barcola then squandered another opportunity when he opted to pass rather than shoot after Liverpool broke forward on the counter-attack.

Perhaps his mind was still on his first-half opportunity, when he intercepted Janelt's attempted header and raced clear, only to lift his effort over the onrushing goalkeeper and wide. Either way, the two chances gave Liverpool fans a glimpse of what may be to come once he settles fully on Merseyside.

Signed from Paris St Germain in a deal worth up to 123 million pounds, the 24-year-old was a constant threat from his starting position on the left wing, cutting inside onto his right foot to shoot or cross and moving infield or up front whenever the opportunity arose.

Vinicius's red card for hair-pulling last weekend provoked ire in the Spanish capital at officiating in Spain.

Mbappe skill

023227dcbcf71c22: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 18 — Toxic haze from wildfires burning in Indonesia has spiked a demand for oxygen tanks and air purifiers across the region, manufacturers say, as they work the clock on equipment providing life-saving clean air.
The months-long haze has blanketed parts of South-east Asia, forcing school closures and fuelling a rise in respiratory complaints. Families are now rushing to buy devices to keep indoor air clean.
At AA Alive, a medical equipment company based just outside of Kuala Lumpur, employees were working at full capacity to deliver oxygen bottles, with officials saying sales were rocketing.
“We have seen a 35 per cent increase in sales because of the haze,” Rafina Firdaus, a member of AA Alive’s sales team, told AFP during a visit.
“When I started in the industry, I was shocked to see so many patients who need oxygen tanks,” she said.
The company supplies patients with both oxygen tanks and oxygen concentrators.
An oxygen tank can run for about three hours of continuous use, while a concentrator can be used for about 24 hours.
Md Noor Bin Bujang, 69, spent more than a month in hospital and received his first oxygen concentrator on Thursday evening.
He told AFP that without the oxygen-providing equipment he would have “a shortness of breath, especially with the haze”.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Md Noor Bin Bujang watches television while using an oxygen concentrator at his home in Rawang. — AFP pic
Mubassar Khan, a 26-year-old AA Alive technician, said an oxygen concentrator’s filter is normally replaced after 1,000 hours of usage, but the haze’s pollutants have halved its lifespan.

AA Alive currently delivers around 40 rental units per day, and Firdaus said the company was able to meet the increased demands caused by the haze because they have “already experienced it every year”.
AFP journalists saw close to 60 oxygen concentrators and around 20 oxygen tanks that were due for a service or replacement at the company’s showroom and warehouse.
‘Sharp surge’
Experts warn prolonged exposure to haze pollutants could cause inflammation that is harmful to the body, with one classifying the situation as a “multisystem public health threat”.

Juliana Jalaludin, a professor specialising in environmental health at Universiti Putra Malaysia, told AFP she was worried that future generations could “experience a higher burden of respiratory illnesses if they are repeatedly exposed to haze and air pollution, particularly during childhood”.
“The key is to reduce exposure now to protect children’s health and prevent long-term consequences for future generations,” Juliana said.
Air purifier retailers, meanwhile, said sales have jumped since air quality levels started to dip in August during haze conditions.

“Recently, we have seen a 600 per cent increase in sale volume of air purifier sales... from September 28 to October 12, compared to the same period last year,” regional consumer electronics retailer Courts said in a statement.
“Customers are becoming more conscious of indoor air quality and are actively exploring solutions to maintain a healthier and more comfortable home environment,” a Courts spokesperson told AFP.
Singapore-based retailer Gain City said it has also seen “a significant increase in air-purifier demand”.

“Demand began picking up in recent weeks, with a particularly sharp surge from October 9. Sales have since risen to nine times the level recorded at the start of the haze season in August,” the company said. — AFP

a800b88c6b881979: LONDON, Oct 18 — On a recent weekend, Laura Latham eagerly swung her racquet on a padel court celebrating one year playing one of the world’s fast-growing sports now taking hold in the UK.
“I hadn’t ever picked up a racquet in my entire life ... and I just fell in love,” the 42-year-old civil servant, who lives in Stockport in northwest England, told AFP.
“I know that sounds a bit cliche, but I was just welcomed into this amazing community of fabulous people, all ages, all shapes and sizes ... It’s just great.”
Latham is among a growing number of padel devotees in Britain, where its popularity has exploded after lagging behind European neighbours.

A cross between tennis and squash played by doubles teams on courts enclosed by glass or wire, enthusiasts see it as an accessible and social sport, while critics say it is an expensive fad for trendsetters.
Other complaints range from the noise to private equity firms funding its expansion, especially in the United States.
Tennis legend Rafael Nadal and football icon Cristiano Ronaldo are among players as well as high-profile investors in the fast-paced game, created in Mexico in the late 1960s.
As the sport has grown rapidly in parts of the world, it has attracted finance from a growing array of sources, from real estate firms to specialised institutional investors.
Its recent UK growth has sparked friction in some places, most notably London, where several sites with new or proposed courts have provoked pushback from local communities.

“It’s a kind of hedge fund-backed sport, taking over local spaces and sports,” complained Agnieszka Wood, 52, who helped spearhead an ultimately unsuccessful campaign to stop a beloved east London skating park becoming padel courts.
“But what happens if there’s too many padel courts? What happens if you’re taking the spaces from the communities and you’re not replacing them?”
‘Hotspots’
Padel’s growing popularity is unquestioned, with Wood acknowledging even her own children enjoy playing it.
The Lawn Tennis Association (LTA), the sport’s governing body in Britain, announced in May that national participation had surpassed one million, with nearly 2,000 courts now open nationwide.
That compares with just 400,000 players and 870 courts at the end of 2024.
Globally, active player numbers climbed last year to nearly 20 million, according to the 2026 Global Padel Report, making it one of the world’s fast-growing sports.
Last month it debuted as a medal sport at the Asian Games and harbours hopes of featuring at the Olympics.

Italy, Spain, Portugal and Argentina — so-called “padel heartlands” — lead the way, while Britain has become one of several “demand-led hotspots”, a report by an arm of the consultancy PwC and sport app Playtomic found.
“Padel is tapping into the UK’s deep racquet-sport heritage,” consultant Ray Algar, who compiled the 2026 UK Padel Report, told AFP.
His report estimates more than half of UK padel courts are in cities with around a quarter in rural places.
‘Losing places’
Soul Padel is among the companies behind Britain’s boom.
It has opened 16 pay-to-play courts across four sites in central and northern England and Scotland, with seven more surfaces to open imminently.
Host towns include post-industrial places like northwestern St Helen’s and Warrington — a long way from the caricature image of where padel is played.
“Our view was that the sport had landed well in the UK but ... within affluent areas and had been pitched to that kind of crowd,” explained Soul Padel’s founder and CEO Mark Hewlett.
They offer various targeted programmes, including “Soul Timers” for over-50s, “Soul Singles” for singletons and its most popular, “Soul Sisters”, for women.
Its court rental costs vary by venue and scheme.
In Stockport, Latham said she pays £11 (RM60) for her share of some off-peak games, rising by around £5 at peak times.
But in London, the cost is typically higher and seen as prohibitive by some.
In Bethnal Green, residents are campaigning against council plans to install a temporary court in an area popular with roller‑skaters, skateboarders and basketball players.
Meanwhile, displaced skaters remain upset about August’s closure of nearby Barking skatepark.
“There was huge, huge opposition from the people who went there,” musician and skater Eleanor Dunlop, 29, who co-led the movement against the change, told AFP.
“We’re definitely losing places, like third spaces, where you can be and there’s not immense pressure to spend money.” — AFP
602b6cde2ae5849b: JERUSALEM, Oct 18 — Three years after suffering their deadliest single attack, Israelis will deliver their verdict on veteran Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in an October 27 election that could decide if the country moves definitively into hard-right nationalism.

The trauma of October 7, 2023 remains raw across Israel. Faded stickers bearing the haunting smiles of young people killed by Hamas cover station walls and lampposts, and at bustling restaurants, no one bats an eye as patrons dine with their assault rifles, now liberally allowed.

Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving prime minister who polls show is in a tight race, is seeking a new mandate after leading a multi-front regional war in response to October 7, with Israel reducing Gaza to rubble, occupying part of Lebanon and, with US help, bombarding Iran.
The relentless Gaza campaign has brought pariah status to Israel in many once-friendly Western countries, and Netanyahu himself faces an arrest warrant from the International Criminal Court.

Even if the public broadly has supported the war’s aims, the effects at home have been much more divisive, including emboldening Netanyahu’s far-right allies bent on reshaping Israel into a religious-nationalist Jewish state.

“I really think that these elections are about the future of the state in a literal sense,” said Gideon Rahat, a political scientist at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem and the Israel Democracy Institute.

Netanyahu’s government has ramped up settlements in the occupied West Bank where settlers armed with the blessing of far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir have been attacking Palestinians on their lands with only occasional pushback from authorities.
“The state without a monopoly on the use of force is a failed state,” Rahat said.
Netanyahu, who turns 77 on October 21, has served as prime minister on and off for more than 19 years.

The wily political operator returned to power in December 2022 bringing in once-shunned ultra-nationalists and quickly tried to rein in the judiciary, which is examining corruption charges that could land him in jail.
The proposed reforms brought out some of the largest protests in Israel’s history in the months before the Hamas attack.
“Everyone in the country has a strong opinion about Netanyahu. People either hate him or adore him,” said Alon Yakter, a political scientist at Tel Aviv University.
“When you want to see who people vote for, the first question you have to ask is their emotional feelings about Netanyahu.”
Anti-Netanyahu in style, not stance
Seeking to unseat Netanyahu is an informal bloc of parties united mostly around their distaste for him.

Netanyahu’s most formidable rival, according to polls, is former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, who is in many ways his antithesis — a political novice who wants to unite centrists rather than rally a base, and a phlegmatic speaker with halting English and none of the American-raised Netanyahu’s flair for blistering, headline-grabbing speeches.
Eisenkot as well as other opposition leaders have zeroed in on why Netanyahu failed to prevent October 7.
Netanyahu has been rocked by reports he ignored warnings. He vehemently denies the charges, blaming security chiefs who he said failed to wake him up that morning.
Netanyahu “may have his perfect English, but even with perfect English he got us October 7”, Eisenkot, in Hebrew, told a security conference at Reichman University.
Eisenkot’s son died in the Gaza war — offering an unspoken contrast to Netanyahu’s son Yair, a globe-trotting social media provocateur.

The working-class son of Moroccan Jewish immigrants, Eisenkot would be the first prime minister of Middle Eastern ancestry, a watershed in a country politically dominated since its founding by an elite of European descent.

Opposition leaders have not criticised Netanyahu’s decision to wage war, likely a losing stance in a country where a recent survey found that only 21 percent of the population identifies as anywhere left of centre.
Eisenkot, as military chief during the 2006 Lebanon war, promoted the Israeli doctrine of using massive force even against civilian infrastructure when in areas used by militants such as Hezbollah.

The opposition has instead heavily focused on social issues including Netanyahu’s tight alliance with ultra-Orthodox Jews, a fast-growing segment of the population due to high birth rates that has promoted religious priorities such as keeping public transit closed on Saturdays.
Netanyahu, while personally secular, has allowed religious students to remain exempt from military service, a source of particular resentment when stretched reservists have served multiple tours.

Opposition figure Naftali Bennett, prime minister in a short-lived 2021-22 government, has vowed to end all exemptions to military service and said that social divisions were putting Israel on a “slow-motion suicide mission”.
Hardline appeal
While the opposition attacks Netanyahu over October 7, for some Israelis, the aftermath of the attack shows the government has brought stability.
While Israelis have died in Iranian and Hezbollah retaliatory attacks, fire has stopped from Gaza, even as Israel keeps striking the territory and Hamas remains.
Israel’s economy has boomed since October 7, with construction sites dotting the major cities and the stock market soaring, led by the technology and defence sectors.

Neriah Yarchi, 19, a barber from Bat Yam near Tel Aviv, came of political age after October 7. He said he would vote for far-right Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, who wants the “voluntary” removal of Gaza’s two million Palestinians.
“If Gaza had been ours, they wouldn’t have had a place to infiltrate from and there wouldn’t have been a massacre,” Yarchi said.

Netanyahu has sought to seize on his international notoriety, with his Likud party putting up posters of leaders including New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, an outspoken critic of Israeli policies, that read, “They want Netanyahu to lose. Don’t let them win.”

Netanyahu has also vowed loudly never to align with parties representing Arab Israelis, who make up around one-fifth of the population and who some expect to turn out in higher numbers after the intense anti-Arab stances of some of Netanyahu’s ministers.
Arab lawmakers broke precedent to be kingmakers in the 2021-2022 government.

If the new election’s results are as close as expected, it could take weeks or months to form a government. Eisenkot has said he would not ally with Arab parties or Netanyahu, but some critics do not believe he would refuse.
Uriel Reichman, a former lawmaker who founded the university bearing his name, told the conference addressed by Eisenkot that a Netanyahu triumph could permanently entrench Israel’s right-wing turn.
He drew a parallel to countries such as Turkey where an elected populist packs the government with loyalists and transforms once-independent institutions.
“Experience shows that once such a system is put in place, it would be extremely difficult to dismantle it,” he said. — AFP
33a39808625dc5d3: IPOH, Oct 18 — For five years, a wheelchair was Salinah Osman’s constant companion, confining the once-active massage therapist to a life far removed from the independence she had enjoyed before suffering a second stroke in 2021.

The 58-year-old, originally from Bukit Mertajam, Penang, still remembers the morning she tried to stand up from a seated position, only for both legs to suddenly give way and her right hand to grow weak.

Unlike her first stroke about two decades earlier, the second robbed her of the strength and mobility she needed to practise her profession, which had brought relief and comfort to hundreds of clients through her home-based spa business.

It also kept her away from the community and volunteer work she loved, leaving her dependent on her husband, Md Rasid Mehat, 66, for daily care while she grappled with other health problems, including heart failure and chronic asthma.

“The ordeal was difficult. I could no longer go out to do charity work, and watching my friends continue with it was heartbreaking. From then on, I had to depend on my husband to take care of me,” she told Bernama.
Despite the setbacks, the mother of two refused to give up, seeking traditional treatments and hospital care while praying for a chance to regain her independence.

Her breakthrough came when she learnt about the rehabilitation benefits available to contributors of the Social Security Organisation (Perkeso) who had suffered strokes, prompting her to submit an application.

In a turn of events she had hardly imagined, contributions she had made while working in a factory more than 20 years ago became the key to accessing the treatment she needed. Although she had long left factory work to become a self-employed massage therapist, her past contributions continued to entitle her to protection under the scheme.
In April, Salinah was offered an intensive rehabilitation programme at the Sultan Nazrin Shah Perkeso Rehabilitation Centre in Meru here, with the cost fully covered by Perkeso.

She spent nearly four months undergoing treatment and staying at the centre, supported by her case manager, medical officers and other staff, while using advanced rehabilitation equipment to help her regain movement and strength.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Salinah progressed from relying on a wheelchair to walking with a stick, before eventually being able to walk unaided after returning home. — Bernama pic
“The desire to get back on my feet kept me going. At first, I had to train for hours every day despite my asthma, and I wondered whether I could do it.

“But one day, I began to move my hand and feel my leg again. That was when I became confident that I could recover here,” said Salinah, who has also been receiving a Perkeso Invalidity Pension since November 2006, which has risen from RM269 to RM573.69 a month.

In the final months of her rehabilitation, she progressed from relying on a wheelchair to taking steps with a walking stick. She also completed a computer networking course to help improve her business when she is ready to resume work.
Salinah was discharged on September 3, and just a week later, while at home, she was able to discard the walking stick and walk without it.

Having gone from being bedridden and fully dependent on a wheelchair to regaining her mobility, she is now working towards rebuilding her massage business and returning to the community service that once formed a major part of her life.

Perkeso chief executive officer Datuk Seri Dr Mohammed Azman Aziz Mohammed said the centre offered comprehensive stroke rehabilitation combining clinical expertise, various therapies and advanced technology, adding that it was open to everyone who required stroke rehabilitation, not just Perkeso contributors.
“For insured persons who meet the eligibility requirements, Perkeso will fully cover rehabilitation costs, subject to an assessment of their condition and suitability for treatment.
“Those who do not qualify for Perkeso benefits may still receive treatment at the centre on a self-funded basis, subject to the same assessment,” he said in a statement to Bernama.

Dr Mohammed Azman said treatment costs varied according to each patient’s condition, needs and rehabilitation goals. The centre offers physiotherapy, occupational therapy, hydrotherapy, speech and swallowing therapy, neuro-robotic rehabilitation, psychological support and vocational rehabilitation, including its Return to Work (RTW) programme.

Its advanced equipment includes the Cyberdyne Hybrid Assistive Limb (HAL), Luna EMG, Vibramoov, MetaMotus Galileo platform and Brain-Computer Interface (BCI), as well as brain neuromodulation technologies such as rTMS and tDCS, and NESA.
He said Perkeso also focused on prevention and long-term protection through its Health Screening Programme, introduced in 2013 to help detect non-communicable disease risks early.

Contributors whose ability to work was impaired by stroke could be considered for benefits under the Invalidity Scheme, including a lifelong Invalidity Pension, Invalidity Grant, Constant Attendance Allowance and rehabilitation aids, subject to medical certification and eligibility requirements. — Bernama
bd3da3eff3ce1dd6: TOKYO, Oct 18 — Japanese scientists are readying a mission to Mars’s moons to retrieve samples that could help unlock the origins of the Solar System and life on Earth, in what aims to be the first-round trip to the Martian region.

The unmanned Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) probe, a collaboration with US and European space agencies as well as numerous universities and tech companies, could also help lay the groundwork for eventual human exploration.
The flagship H3 rocket carrying the MMX is set to blast off from the Tanegashima Space Centre Tuesday at 4:41am (1941 GMT Monday), according to the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (Jaxa).

The spacecraft will arrive near Mars one year later, where it will orbit its moon Phobos for up to three years before landing and collecting at least 10 grams (0.35 ounces) of material from the surface.
A rover dubbed IDEFIX — the French name for the comic hero Asterix’s dog — will first conduct surface observations aimed at ensuring a safe landing.
“The sampling (from) Phobos is of course the world’s first, but it means... this is the first round-trip to the Martian system,” MMX’s project manager Yasuhiro Kawakatsu told AFP.

Jaxa said the mission will also explore the possibility of using Phobos as a “natural space station” by establishing the requirements for a round trip to Mars — something “essential for crewed Mars exploration”.
It will also observe the Red Planet’s moon Deimos, although it will not land on it, before returning to Earth.
Impact or capture
Jaxa hopes the mission will reveal how Mars and its two moons formed, a key piece of knowledge in working out how the Solar System was born.
One theory for the origin of the Martian moons — the “giant impact” hypothesis — is that they formed after a celestial body collided with Mars.
The “capture” hypothesis, meanwhile, postulates that the moons are asteroids captured by Mars’s gravity.

Determining which is right will help reveal “how a habitable environment for life might have arisen on the terrestrial planets”, Jaxa said, referring to the four rocky worlds closest to the Sun — Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars.

“MMX will shed light on the transport mechanisms that delivered water, volatiles, and organic compounds from the outer Solar System to the inner rocky planet region — processes that may have played a key role in making these worlds habitable,” said Patrick Michel, a French astrophysicist working on IDEFIX.

“If Phobos and Deimos are indeed remnants of these early delivery systems, they may hold clues to the origins of life itself, or, to be more correct, to the transport of the materials that were key to the emergence of life on rocky planets,” he told AFP.
Deep in the ‘gravity well’
MMX is a collaboration with France’s National Centre for Space Studies (CNES), the German Aerospace Center (DLR), Nasa, the European Space Agency (ESA), and about 20 universities and tech companies.
The development of the spacecraft’s landing legs was particularly difficult, as gravity on Phobos is extremely weak, Jaxa scientists say.

Japan’s unmanned Smart Lander for Investigating Moon (SLIM) — the “Moon Sniper” — tipped over after touching down on Earth’s Moon in 2024, but still transmitted data and survived several two-week lunar nights.

Japan also has experience in bringing back samples from space, including Jaxa’s unmanned Hayabusa-2, which returned 5.4 grams of rock and dust collected from an asteroid several hundred million kilometres from Earth in 2020.

One of the differences between Jaxa’s past asteroid probes and the MMX mission is that this time “we have to travel very close to Mars and return”, which means escaping the planet’s heavy gravity, Kawakatsu told reporters.
Phobos orbits about 6,000 kilometres above the Martian surface.
“Going deep into what we call the ‘gravity well’ is difficult,” Kawakatsu said.
China’s mission
US and Chinese space agencies have been racing to be the first to return rock samples from Mars’s surface back to Earth.
Nasa’s Perseverance rover, which has been roaming the Red Planet since 2021, has already collected samples.
The mission, however, was effectively cancelled by the administration of President Donald Trump following a vote by the US Congress in January.
China, meanwhile, has announced its Tianwen-3 spacecraft is scheduled for launch around 2028 and hopes to return Mars samples to Earth as early as 2031 — potentially before the MMX’s return.

Jaxa scientists say sand and rocks from Phobos may offer a wider variety of samples than those on the planet itself, especially if it was formed by a collision between a celestial body and Mars. — AFP

47aeb4577d5d685b: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 18 — Malaysia’s Pearly Tan and M. Thinaah ended an 18-year wait for a women’s doubles title at the Denmark Open today after sweeping aside Japan’s Hinata Suzuki and Nao Yamakita in straight games.
The world No. 5 pair produced a commanding performance to defeat their 21st-ranked opponents 21-18, 21-11 in the final at the SJF Bank Arena in Odense, securing their second title of the season.
The victory made Tan-Thinaah the first Malaysian women’s doubles pair to lift the Denmark Open crown since Wong Pei Tty and Chin Eei Hui achieved the feat in 2008.
It also marked a welcome return to the top of the podium for the Malaysian stars, who had not won a title since January.
Tan-Thinaah were made to work in the opening game against the Japanese pair but held their nerve to take it 21-18.
They then stepped up a gear in the second, dominating their opponents to seal a convincing 21-11 win and complete their historic triumph.
The result was particularly satisfying after their previous title at the Indonesia Masters in Jakarta came without a final being played.
On that occasion, Tan-Thinaah were awarded the championship following the withdrawal of Japan’s Arisa Igarashi and Miyu Takahashi, who handed the Malaysians a walkover.
This time, however, the Malaysian duo claimed the title on court, capping an impressive campaign at the prestigious Super 750 tournament.

Their road to the final included a hard-fought comeback victory over India’s Treesa Jolly and Gayatri Gopichand in the quarter-finals, before they dispatched China’s Bao Li Jing and Cao Zi Han 21-16, 21-14 in Saturday’s semi-final.
The triumph also saw Tan-Thinaah follow in the footsteps of Wong and Chin, who defeated Indonesia’s Rani Mundiasti and Jo Novita 23-21, 21-12 to win the women’s doubles title in 2008.
Eighteen years later, the Denmark Open women’s doubles crown is finally back in Malaysian hands.
4b0885dbd929676e: LEEDS, Oct 18 — Lisandro Martinez was named in Manchester United’s starting line-up to face Leeds today despite his controversial remarks about the struggling club’s hierarchy.
Argentina defender Martinez took aim at United’s powerbrokers following their 2-0 Champions League loss to Atletico Madrid on Tuesday.
Martinez claimed United boss Michael Carrick had been left with an under-strength squad.

The centre-back criticised technical director Jason Wilcox, saying he had “100 per cent” expected more investment during the summer transfer window after United finished third in the Premier League last season.
It is understood Martinez, who issued an apology on Thursday, has been fined for his outburst.
Carrick confirmed during a pre-match press conference on Friday that Martinez would be in his squad for their Premier League match at bitter rivals Leeds.
And he was true to his word as Martinez was selected in a United team looking to win for just the third time in 10 games this term.
United have gone five matches without a victory in all competitions and are languishing in 14th place in the Premier League.
A defeat at Leeds would heap more pressure on Carrick ahead of Wednesday’s Champions League trip to Como. — AFP
d3f3e31c5610d2b3: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 18 — Most temporary flood relief centres (PPS) in Penang, Pahang, Kedah and Perak were closed today as floods improved, with only two remaining in operation in Perak as of 4pm.

In PENANG, Seberang Perai Tengah district officer Datuk Kamarul Haizal Koderat said the only centre at Sekolah Kebangsaan (SK) Seri Penanti in Bukit Mertajam was closed this afternoon, and all 36 victims from 10 families were allowed to return home.
He said the closure followed assessments by the Malaysian Fire and Rescue Department and the Malaysian Civil Defence Force, which found the affected area safe for residents to return.
The centre was opened at 8.30pm last night to house evacuees from Kampung Kubang Semang after their homes were flooded due to heavy rain.
In PAHANG, two PPS in Raub housing 26 evacuees from 11 families were also closed at 1pm today.

The Raub District Disaster Management Committee secretariat said all evacuees at Balai Raya Kampung Baru Cheroh and Balai Raya Sempam Baru PPS had been allowed to return home as flood conditions continued to improve.

In PERAK, Larut, Matang dan Selama District Disaster Management Committee chairman Mohd Nasrul Menhat said three PPS, at SK Changkat Ibol, Dewan Masjid Al-Wusta Batu 8 and Dewan Perdana Trong, were closed at 1.30pm today.
However, the Perak State Disaster Management Committee secretariat said two PPS remained in operation as of 4pm, at SK Matang Gelugor and SK Matang.

The floods hit Kampung Matang Pasir and Kampung Matang Gelugor, while the storm also struck Kampung Changkat Baru Matang, Kampung Teluk Kertam, Kampung Melawati and Kampung Hujung Matang.
Other areas also hit by floods were Kampung Changkat Ibol, Kampung Batu 9 and the Trong and Matang areas.

In a related development, Higher Education Minister Datuk Seri Dr Zambry Abd Kadir said in a Facebook post that he had visited flood-hit areas in Pulau Pangkor today, but no PPS had been opened on the island so far. — Bernama

0bc6c3351b2b4b81: SHANGHAI, Oct 18 — Alejandro Davidovich Fokina fought back to beat rising star Rafael Jodar in the final of the Shanghai Masters today to claim the biggest title of his career.
The gutsy world number 26 from Spain outlasted his tiring compatriot 1-6, 7-6 (7/5), 6-4.
“I don’t know what to say. I don’t know what I feel. Just like a huge relief,” Davidovich Fokina said.
It is a first title at the prestigious 1000 level for the 27-year-old, who extended his winning streak in China to 10 matches after claiming victory at an ATP 250 tournament in Chengdu.
The 20-year-old Jodar, ranked 13 and rising fast, was ruthless to start with.
He reached over his shoulder to save a point before winning it with an overhead smash as he broke for a 2-0 lead.
Davidovich Fokina put pressure on his backhand, but Jodar kept calm as his opponent succumbed to a series of errors.
Jodar broke again to go up 5-1 before closing out the first set after just 27 minutes with an ace.
A fighting Davidovich Fokina refused to go away.
He dropped serve to hand Jodar a 3-2 lead in the second set but finally came up with some answers in the next game, falling on his back to save a point at the net and level at 3-3.
Both men battled to hold serve in a run of intense rallies, with the duo needing to restart a point during the ninth game when a ball rolled onto the court.
Davidovich Fokina was shouting in frustration but saved two break points to go up 6-5 when Jodar returned into the net.
But the younger Spaniard would not crumble, sending down a dangerous backhand to force a tie-break.
The duo were neck and neck but Davidovich Fokina held his nerve in the tie-break to force a decider.
He was suddenly in control, breaking Jodar’s serve in the first game.
His celebration was cut short when Jodar grabbed back a break.
But it went his way again when Jodar fired long to hand the elder Spaniard a 3-2 lead.
Jodar needed a medical timeout for his right thigh as he trailed Davidovich Fokina 4-3.
He buckled in pain as he went for a point during a must-win ninth game, keeping the match alive for a bit longer but needing a trainer for his left thigh at 5-4.
Davidovich Fokina sensed victory and claimed the title on his second championship point. — AFP
21062fe420102790: KUALA TERENGGANU, Oct 18 — Department heads in the public service sector can leverage the Hybrid Workday (HBH) Policy to adapt to haze conditions in their respective states.

Public Service Department (PSD) director-general Tan Sri Dr Wan Ahmad Dahlan Abdul Aziz said that department heads may employ appropriate methods under the HBH framework to ensure that work deliverables or Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) for every civil servant are met.
“We have already implemented this hybrid work schedule, and in the context of the current haze, it is essentially a matter of the situation coinciding.

“Therefore, it is up to the department heads to make use of this arrangement. We can certainly utilise the HBH Policy. However, the most important aspect is that KPIs must be established to ensure that output is maintained, even when working in a hybrid manner during these haze conditions,” he said following the ‘Santuni Pesara’ programme held around Kuala Terengganu and Kuala Nerus today.
Also present was the Terengganu Federal Development Department director Datuk Abdul Kahar Abdul Latif.

During the programme, Wan Ahmad Dahlan took the time to visit and present cash contributions as well as basic necessities to three families of retired government servants — Soh Kim Seah, 90; and Rosnani Abdullah, 73; and Mohd Saadum Che Embong, 69.

Meanwhile, he said that the provision of a special financial assistance of RM750 to over one million government retirees, as outlined in Budget 2027, demonstrates the government’s concern for the contributions made by this group.
He noted that the contributions of retirees to national development throughout their years of service are of immense value and should not be forgotten.

“This clearly shows that the government has never neglected retirees who have served the nation. The ‘Santuni Pesara’ programme is also one of the initiatives implemented to honour their contributions,” he added. — Bernama
632ea8a3cf541431: TAIPEI, Oct 18 — Taiwan said today it had driven away 16 Chinese coast guard, research and fishing vessels involved in simultaneous “maritime harassment” operations.

An “unusually large” number of Chinese vessels took part in the coordinated operations around Taiwan’s main island and Pratas, a disputed island to the southwest, the Taiwanese coast guard said in a statement.
The Chinese vessels, including four fishing boats, carried out “simultaneous operations at multiple locations and engaged in hybrid warfare,” the statement said.
The locations were off Taiwan’s eastern, southern and southwestern coastlines, and around Pratas. Some of the Chinese vessels entered Taiwan’s restricted waters.
Beijing claims Taiwan is part of its territory and also asserts jurisdiction over the waters around the island, which Taipei rejects. China has long threatened to use force to seize Taiwan.
China has intensified its maritime pressure on Taiwan in recent months, deploying record numbers of coast guard, research and other vessels around the island.

Today’s operation comes after Taiwan’s coast guard used a water cannon against a Chinese recreational fishing vessel near Pratas, in the northern part of the South China Sea, on October 1, which sparked an angry response from China.
Taiwan controls Pratas, also known as Dongsha, but Beijing also claims the island along with most of the strategic waterway.
Taiwan’s coast guard said its vessels took “forceful action immediately to effectively neutralise the threats”.
“China is attempting to unilaterally alter the status quo across the Taiwan Strait and create the false impression of jurisdiction,” the statement said.
“Such actions will only lead to resentment among the people of Taiwan, and the Coast Guard Administration condemns them in the strongest terms.”
China began conducting law enforcement patrols in waters to the east of Taiwan in June, which Taipei branded as “provocative” and “expansionism in disguise”.
Beijing has since dialled up pressure, deploying a record 244 coast guard, scientific research and other ships around Taiwan’s main island in July, Taiwanese official data show.
That compares with 55 ships detected in June and 30 in May, and 58 in July last year. In the first 21 days of August, 152 vessels were detected.
About 60 per cent are coast guard ships, with research vessels and other government boats making up the rest.
The figures do not include Chinese warships, which China’s military deploys around Taiwan on a near-daily basis. — AFP
8e6e1b3a66655ed7: KUDAT, Oct 18 — The RM18.7 billion allocated to Sabah under Budget 2027 is not solely for development projects, but also covers the operating costs of federal ministries and departments in the state, Sabah Finance Minister Datuk Seri Masidi Manjun said.
He said a large portion of the allocation will cover operating expenses, including salaries for about 120,000 federal civil servants working in Sabah.
Masidi said the Education and Health departments are the largest recipients of operating funds, together accounting for more than half of the RM18.7 billion allocation.
“The RM18.7 billion is not entirely for development. We need to understand that the allocation also covers the operating costs of federal ministries and departments operating in Sabah.

“So, it would be inaccurate to assume that the entire RM18.7 billion allocation is intended to address water supply problems and other development needs in the state,” he told reporters on the sidelines of the Gabungan Rakyat Sabah (GRS) 2026 Convention here today.
According to him, the budget’s development allocation includes funding for both new projects and the continuation of existing projects currently under way.
He added that Sabah’s development needs continue to grow each year, and existing allocations may not be enough to resolve the state’s long-standing infrastructure problems. — Bernama
2c73297beacfa5b2: ROME, Oct 18 — Pope Leo XIV addressed thousands of people in St Peter’s Square today, smiling and saying he would resume work “gradually” in his first major public appearance since undergoing lung cancer surgery.
The 71-year-old pope had part of his right lung removed in the surgery on Tuesday at Rome’s Gemelli hospital and he was discharged yesterday.
“I would like to thank all the people who have been praying for me in these days,” the leader of the world’s 1.4 billion Catholics told the crowd.
“Having overcome this delicate phase, as you know I will now gradually resume my activities,” said the pope, who looked well and spoke normally.
A chorus of “Viva il papa!” (Hooray for the pope!) had reverberated across the square as he appeared at the window of his Apostolic Palace for his traditional Angelus prayer and address.
People in the square welcomed the pope’s speedy return.
Christopher Butler, 68, a parish priest from Leeds in northern England called Leo a “great shepherd for the Catholic Church”.
“I’m concerned he needs to take time to make a full recovery but he’s obviously a very resilient man and keen to return to work, to lead the Church and to be a world leader,” Butler said.
Soledad Espinosa, 59, from Ecuador, said she was happy to hear that the pope would be allowed by his doctors to visit Latin America next month.
“We are all hoping for his recovery and that he has gotten through the situation well. We know that he is ok and we’re pleased,” she said.
Norma Grasso, 76, from Argentina, said: “We are waiting for him”.
Following the surgery, there had been doubts about a planned papal voyage scheduled for November 6-17, to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, where Leo spent two decades as a missionary.
But his surgeon, Stefano Margaritora, told Vatican News he believed there were “no clinical reasons why the trip should not go ahead”.
‘Absolutely satisfactory’
The pope’s discharge yesterday capped days of uncertainty that rattled the Vatican and the world’s Catholics, less than two years into the Chicago-born pope’s papacy.
Margaritora said Leo was in “absolutely satisfactory clinical condition,” estimating another 10 days before he is fully recovered.
Margaritora told Vatican News that Leo’s tumour had been discovered by chance, during a routine abdominal X-ray that captured the “little spot” at the base of his right lung.
While calling the lung operation “routine”, he saluted the pope’s commitment to his recovery, saying he “really put his heart and soul into it, like the most motivated patients”.
“His determination to achieve a very quick and very effective recovery from every point of view was really commendable,” Margaritora said.
The results of tests to determine whether the cancer has spread are still pending.
Leo has resumed some work, making a call on Friday to Russian President Vladimir Putin to urge a ceasefire in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky. — AFP
bfa20c62b8bb1167: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 18 — Japan’s yuzu, prized for its distinctive fragrance and citrusy tang, is emerging as a potential addition to Malaysia’s halal market, with producers from Kochi Prefecture eyeing new export opportunities.

Director of the Kochi Representative Office in Singapore, Akihisa Ikeda, said Kochi Prefecture participated in the Malaysia International Halal Showcase (Mihas 2026) under the Japan Pavilion, showcasing products that have obtained halal certification.
“While some yuzu products from Kochi Prefecture are already being exported to Malaysia, there are still many untapped opportunities in other sectors.
“This is our first time participating in Mihas, as we seek to tap into the growing demand for halal food,” he told Bernama on the sidelines of Mihas 2026 recently.

Two companies from Kochi Prefecture participated in the event, namely Kochi Ice Co Ltd, which manufactures desserts using yuzu and other citrus fruits, and Umaji Village Agricultural Cooperative, which represents yuzu farmers.
Ikeda said yuzu-based products, which are already popular in Asean countries, still have room for growth.
“Singapore is the first country in Asia to import yuzu products from Japan, and in Thailand, there are many cafes that serve yuzu-flavoured drinks,” he said.
In Malaysia, halal-certified frozen desserts made with yuzu juice from Kochi Prefecture are already sold in Japanese restaurants, he said.
“Yuzu drink and jam from the Umaji Village Agricultural Cooperative are also available in retail outlets in Malaysia, and all these products are halal-certified.

“While most of these yuzu products from Japan are still relatively new in Malaysia, in Europe, especially in France, it is known as a culinary sensation among chefs as they use yuzu seasoning and condiments to enhance flavours in dishes,” Ikeda said.

The Kochi Prefecture, a major yuzu producer in Japan, has been expanding its export market in Europe and the United States, and is now eyeing a larger market share in Asian countries, including Malaysia and Singapore.
According to Ikeda, the producers are targeting consumers who can understand and appreciate the quality and unique features of Kochi’s yuzu produce.

“The fruits are cultivated in the mountain areas of Kochi villages in an ideal environment that produces yuzu fruit with a strong aroma, which is then processed into yuzu-based beverages and seasonings for exports.

“Therefore, there would be no adjustments to price at the moment in spite of rising costs of packaging and other raw materials, as the emphasis would be on maintaining the quality of yuzu-based products from Kochi,” he added.
Ikeda said the producers are focusing on expanding distribution channels in Malaysia, encouraged by the positive market reaction to Japanese yuzu-based products. — Bernama
ab68d03e47fd3127: SINGAPORE, Oct 18 — Residents in Singapore enjoyed a rare day of clearer skies and fresher air today, after a change in wind directions led to an improvement in air quality here.
In its daily haze situation update this evening, the National Environment Agency (NEA) stated that winds had turned to blow from the south.
“However, some smoke haze from Kalimantan continued drifting towards Singapore. Smoke haze was also observed over Sumatra,” the agency said.
At 6pm, the one-hour PM2.5 was in the normal band in the northern region (36), while remaining in the low-elevated band in eastern (67), central (69), western (66) and southern (69) Singapore.

a8370965b9965830: BANGKOK, Oct 18 — Thai authorities have warned of possible flash floods and landslides across Bangkok and 35 provinces as heavy to very heavy rain threatens large parts of the country until October 25.
The Thai Meteorological Department said the wet weather would initially affect southern and eastern Thailand before spreading to Bangkok, central Thailand and other regions from October 21 to 25.

The warning comes as Thailand’s Department of Disaster Prevention and Mitigation (DDPM) placed 35 provinces and the capital on alert, with local authorities instructed to prepare emergency response teams and equipment, according to The Nation.
Persistent rainfall is forecast in the south and east from October 18 to 20, with some areas expected to experience heavy to very heavy downpours.

From October 21, rainfall is expected to intensify across the lower northeast, central region, including Bangkok and surrounding provinces, the east and upper south, accompanied by occasional strong gusts of wind.

The department warned that prolonged rainfall could trigger flash floods, sudden runoff from higher ground and landslides, particularly in low-lying areas and communities near foothills and waterways.
Residents have been urged to monitor weather updates and avoid roads prone to repeated flooding.

According to The Nation, eastern provinces including Chonburi and Rayong could face very heavy rainfall on October 21 and 22, while southern tourist destinations such as Phuket, Phang Nga and Krabi are forecast to experience intense downpours later in the week.
The meteorological department has also warned of hazardous conditions at sea, with waves potentially exceeding three metres during thunderstorms in the Andaman Sea and Gulf of Thailand.
Boats have been advised to navigate cautiously and avoid areas affected by thunderstorms.
The unsettled weather is being driven by a monsoon trough over southern Thailand and the southwest monsoon affecting the lower Andaman Sea.
The trough is expected to shift northwards as a high-pressure system from China extends over northern and northeastern Thailand and the South China Sea.

Thailand has already experienced widespread flooding in recent weeks. According to Reuters, floods had killed 71 people since September 16 and affected 51 provinces as of October 12, with about 908,000 households affected.
The latest warning comes as Thailand transitions from its rainy season towards the cooler months, when shifting weather systems can still bring heavy rainfall.
Authorities have urged residents in affected areas to remain vigilant and follow official weather advisories.

21e8899f3f3dee8c: The Windows command line is a marvelous thing, beloved by administrators, but not quite so welcome when you're trying to get a parcel out of a locker. Today's example of Windows behaving badly comes from Ireland and one of the nation's OOHPod postal lockers. An eagle-eyed Register reader, trying to retrieve a parcel, found the locker screen instead teasing a command prompt. For the uninitiated, OOHPod is a service where people retrieve and deposit goods in lockers. Scan your ID (or enter it on a touch screen) and the appropriate locker door springs open and the item (or items) can be retrieved. This all works, assuming whatever is running behind the scenes isn't having a bit of a moment, as our reader experienced. Instead of a welcoming display on the locker's screen, our reader found a blank screen and what looked suspiciously like a minimized command-line window. "I tapped to maximize the window," they told us, "and a sudden command prompt appeared immediately afterward." A command prompt? More like an open invitation for mischief for the average Register reader. After all, while ordinary customers might have been flustered, this was surely an opportunity to teach the engineers who allowed it a lesson. Perhaps a cheeky FORMAT, or possibly the creation of a truly cursed batch file? Or something worse? This is surely what the comment section is made for. Unfortunately (or fortunately, depending on your perspective), no pop-up keyboard appeared for our reader to unleash havoc (not that they would dream of such a thing), and there was no handy socket to plug in a peripheral. The touchscreen accepted another finger jab, and the command window went away, replaced by the usual OOHPod interface, allowing packages to be collected as normal. It was the responsible thing to do, and the bank of lockers was left in a state where the next customer would not have to worry about what this odd cmd.exe thing was all about. However, the question remains. Would you have been so responsible? Or, if there was some way to enter commands, would you have tried to turn a minor bork into a life lesson for the engineer who let Windows give passersby a glimpse of its undercrackers? ®

631c78f18e2760a2: In principle, artificial intelligence could make finding the right material for an application as simple as ordering dinner: Scientists would tell a large language model what they want, and it would serve them the perfect material for the job. Unfortunately, that approach doesn’t work well yet, and the problem comes down to data: Most materials consist of 3D arrangements of crystals, not the text streams that today’s large language models are trained on. The experimental literature is also heavily biased toward a few popular classes of crystals, making AI outputs skew toward those materials. Now MIT researchers have created a multimodal AI model that tackles these problems. The model combines 3D atomic structures with natural language descriptions to create rich linguistic descriptions about the structures from experimental research papers and first-principles computational databases. The unified description outlines not just the chemical composition and structure, but also its properties, processing considerations, and potential applications, helping AI learn more about what makes materials impactful. In a new paper in Nature Communications, the researchers showed their system could identify better material designs than models trained on text streams alone by allowing the model to “see” the atomic arrangements and bonding patterns. For example, when the researchers asked the model to identify materials suited for solid-state lithium-ion battery electrolytes, its top results included materials that had been independently identified as promising candidates. The researchers also showed their model learned geometric representations of material structures in ways text-only models could not. “Structure is really at the heart of the materials science field,” says Ju Li, the Carl Richard Soderberg Professor in Power Engineering in the Department of Materials Science and Engineering (DMSE). “If you understand the structure, you can infer quite a lot about the properties and performance of materials. We wanted to build the connection between a material’s atomic structure and its properties and processing for the model.” Joining Li on a paper about the model are Yang Jeong Park, first author and former MIT postdoc; Mayank Kumaran, a recent University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign computer engineering graduate; Chia-Wei Hsu SM ’26; and Elsa Olivetti, the Jerry McAfee (1940) Professor in Engineering in DMSE. Getting models to see in 3D Materials scientists are always on the hunt for new crystals that will lead to the products of the future. Over the last decade, AI has reshaped that process, proposing and designing new crystalline structures, which have highly ordered atomic structures and make up more than 90 percent of solid materials on Earth. Most of those models treat solid crystalline materials as 3D graphs. The rise of large language models has given researchers another tool for innovation. But existing large language models rely heavily on text from published papers and books, limiting their knowledge of the physical world, since many potential crystal structures are stored in computational databases. Text-based models also lack understanding of visual geometry. To overcome those challenges, the researchers decided to create a vision-language model for crystalline materials. They trained a language model to create textual descriptions of crystal structures using an approach known as contrastive learning, in which models compare similar and dissimilar examples of structures and textual descriptions to achieve a unified understanding. This is similar to aligning the visual and language regions of the brain. Following training, the researchers compared the predictions of two versions of the model: one trained on a dataset containing the AI-generated descriptions and the other trained on a dataset containing text from papers only. They found that the model trained on AI-generated descriptions successfully learned how to align geometric structures with text descriptions while the other did not. “We wanted to create an AI model that works broadly across materials,” Li says. “That’s why we decided to synthesize narratives rather than rely solely on existing papers. We found when we used that narrative dataset, the models are better at predicting the function.” Accelerating materials science The researchers then showed their model could be given a natural language query describing a property and identify crystalline materials with that property, outperforming a baseline. “There are sometimes these step changes within materials science around algorithmic integration toward useful tools, which the community uses to further advance the field,” Olivetti says. “This approach helps us see more deeply into three-dimensional structures and link structures to property and processing. I hope this can be one of those step changes.” Li compares the model to AlphaFold, an AI model that links protein structures with function that has helped advance biological research and drug development. The researchers believe their new approach can work with many crystalline materials, and they hope other material scientists will use it to accelerate their work. “Being able to see a three-dimensional crystal and how its atoms are connected is super foundational,” Li says. “I think this will be useful to anyone who practices materials science.” The work was supported, in part, by the U.S. Defense Threat Reduction Agency through the University Research Alliance; the U.S. Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency; and the National Research Foundation of Korea.

4a57d3c28cf22595: I’m not shocked by the revelation that some children are refusing to sit next to their Christian or Muslim classmates. I knew it was coming.
On Oct 15, Puncak Borneo MP Willie Mongin raised concerns in the Dewan Rakyat about religious intolerance among primary school children.
He said a teacher told him that some children said: “I don’t want to sit with them because they eat pork,” or “I don’t want to sit with them because they wear a cross”.

This is far more than a classroom management problem. It is a symptom of a society that is quietly fracturing along ethnic and religious lines — and in Malaysia’s multiethnic reality, that fracture is a national security threat.

In a country where the delicate balance between the Malay-Muslim majority and the Chinese, Indian, and indigenous minorities has historically been the cornerstone of stability, the early crystallisation of “us versus them” at the primary-school level is terribly dangerous, to say the least.

When children are socialised to view difference as a threat rather than a shared reality, the foundation of our society — the mutual accommodation that has kept us together for decades — begins to crumble before critical thinking even develops.
As Mongin warned, if this trend is not addressed at the youngest age, it will inevitably spread, feeding the very 3R controversies that have destabilised Malaysian politics in recent years.
This should not be treated as an isolated case for it reflects deeper structural patterns that threaten Malaysia’s unity.

It is dangerous because it erodes the trust and understanding that underpin social relations, business partnerships and even political alliances. Worse, it creates a radicalisation pipeline: isolated children become vulnerable to extremist online narratives.
I said I knew it was coming. The rise of ethno-religious nationalism, especially since the early 2000s, has amplified our differences.

When an increasing number of politicians unashamedly fire up religion- or race-related issues to win votes or to be seen as champions of their race or religion — and then get away with it or are cheered on by their supporters — what do you expect to happen?
Political rhetoric often frames racial and religious purity as mobilisation tools, and children absorb the tone of such public discourse.
Another reason is that the different communities have moved into their own silos, interacting at work, in school and elsewhere only when and where necessary.

And unlike in the past, the norm today is for children to play or share activities with those of their own race. When school is the only mixed space, and that space is already poisoned by home prejudices or online content, the classroom turns into a battleground instead of a bridge.

Digital poisoning makes the problem worse. Some social media platforms prioritise outrage, with algorithms amplifying hate speech and fake news. Children encounter dehumanising content that normalises rejection of the “other.”
When a pupil says, “I don’t want to sit with them because they wear a cross,” they may have internalised a viral meme or attack on that symbol.
I can go on, but all of us know there are many unspeakable elephants in the room that authorities need to address.
Existing “unity” programmes are well-intentioned but episodic and top-down. They rely on short camps or lectures rather than daily, sustained interaction.

Without structural changes in curriculum and teacher training, they will continue to fail in shifting deep prejudices. Teacher training must include conflict resolution and intercultural communication. Remedies must be structural, not performative as they have been.

Curriculum reform should prioritise critical thinking, media literacy and emotional intelligence over rote “unity” modules. Students need to learn how to deconstruct hate speech and engage in dialogue.
Schools need more group activities to build positive associations.
Digital literacy must become a core subject, not an add-on. Perhaps workshops can be organised for parents on how to guide their children’s online consumption.
Government and civil society must emphasize shared third spaces — mixed sports leagues, arts programmes and community projects — to generate organic positive interactions.
Above all, political leaders must stop exploiting religious and racial divisions for gain. Rhetoric that validates children’s prejudices undermines the very unity they are supposed to defend.

The refusal by six-year-olds to share a desk is small in scale but carries enormous weight. It is a snapshot of Malaysia at a crossroads. If treated as a minor issue, the country risks losing its social cohesion entirely.
If addressed with serious, structural reforms in education, digital literacy and political leadership, genuine unity may be possible.

In a multiethnic society, separation is not merely a social preference — it is a national security threat. Malaysia cannot afford to let its youngest generation grow up believing that difference is a threat rather than a shared reality. The time for action is now.
